To gain a deeper understanding of processes beyond the Standard Model, particularly those involving flavor-changing neutral currents, B meson decay rates are crucial, especially the comparison between B^0_s and B^0_d meson decay rates or the ratio of their decay probabilities. Next-generation experiments, such as LHCb, require highly precise knowledge of the B^0_s meson decay time, as even the. 1% uncertainty in the B^0_s meson decay time corresponds to a significant, 0. 1% uncertainty in the ratio of the probabilities. This research describes multiple, independent, theoretical approaches to assessing the B^0_s meson decay time, all stemming from quantum chromodynamics, and aims to provide the most reliable, independent estimates while providing valuable insights for LHCb in the coming years.

This study examines the discretization of a class of stochastic control problems for which pathwise methods of solving the associated Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation are applicable. It offers a proof of convergence for the approximate control problem and establishes a rate of convergence under specific conditions. Furthermore, this work relates to the robustness of the original problem and its approximations, ultimately contributing to the feasible computation of the value function and optimal feedback solution.

The correlation between the $R_{p p}$ or $R_{d d}$ variation and the centrality of collisions observed in proton-proton, proton-lead and lead-lead collisions at a energy of $7.52$ TeV is investigated using reconstructed di-electron and dipron pairs with a mass range of $2.0$ to $6.0$ GeV. Findings from this study are consistent with the results from previous analyses conducted in proton-proton and proton-lead collisions but diverge from lepton yield measurements in central heavy ion collisions.

In this investigation, we transform the equivalent formulations of noncommutative quantum mechanics proposed by M. Mizrahi and J. Berman into a framework featuring a truly flat, commuting momentum space. Our formulation enables the expression of noncommutative coordinates as first-order differential operators acting within momentum space. Furthermore, these relationships can be seamlessly extended to incorporate the effects of spin through the utilization of Clifford algebras.

The primary objective of this research is to develop a framework that can accurately identify and locate tumor infiltrating lymphocytes within digitized cancer tissue samples. Tumor infiltrating lymphocytes are tumor cells that have been invaded by immune system cells known as lymphocytes. These are critical to understanding the field of cancer immunotherapy. We evaluated our proposed method using three datasets: one publicly available and two privately held. A publicly available dataset, along with a privately available dataset from H. Lee Moffitt Cancer Center & Research Institute, and another from Shanghai Medical Center, Fu Wai Hospital, Beijing Chao Yang Hospital. We experimented with multiple lymphocyte tumor identifier configurations, as well as different lymphocyte and tumor region detection algorithms. We found that using the same algorithm to identify both tumor and lymphocytes yielded the best performance. To optimize the results, a combination of random forest and U-Net algorithms was determined to be the most effective. The most impressive outcome of our research is an overall accuracy rate of 82.5%, achieved with 10% annotation data. This high accuracy is comparable to the performance of human experts, which is 84.5%. Furthermore, our model exhibits strong generalization capabilities, as it was trained on one dataset and then tested on two other datasets with similar results.

This paper proposes an iterative decoding technique for optical communications systems that combines the joint equalization and list-sequence estimation (WDFE) method with MLSE to address the issue of burst errors. By incorporating MLSE to regenerate reliable codewords, the proposed algorithm enhances the system's performance. A theoretical analysis of the mean field equations with MLSE is provided, and a gain in simulation results is observed.

As a robust and versatile tool for various tasks, including time-series forecasting, natural language processing, and audio processing, the Temporal Convolutional Network (TCN) has seen significant success. However, the unoptimized nature of TCNs has led to inefficient implementations with larger model sizes and increased inference time. In response, our research introduces an innovative automatic dilation optimizer for customizing and optimizing the structure of TCNs in a end-to-end manner. By introducing techniques such as asymmetric group dilations, our method tailors the optimizer to reduce both model parameters and inference time while maintaining or enhancing overall performance. The optimized TCN models demonstrate significant improvements in downstream tasks, particularly in few-shot classification and multi-granularity audio classification, with up to a 24.1% reduction in models parameters and a 1.35x decrease in inference time. The optimizer's code is openly available for others to replicate and build upon at https://github.com/airaria/dilation-optimizer-.

This paper provides a comprehensive investigation into the properties of Zinbiel algebras, specifically focusing on lower central series, nilpotency, and solvability. A key contribution is a set of formulas for calculating the dimensions of the derived and lower central series bases in finite-dimensional Zinbiel algebras. Additionally, the paper establishes relationships between these algorithms and the nilpotency or solvability of these algebras. Notably, it demonstrates that all two-generated Zinbiel algebras are nilpotent. The research also compares the structural characteristics of Lie, Leibniz, and Zinbiel algebras.

The quark-gluon plasma formed in heavy-ion collisions at top energy exhibits an unexpected discrepancy between its macroscopic smoothness and microscopic turbulence due to flow patterns. Using initial and final particle data from lead-lead collisions in 2.76 TeV LHC runs, we found that final state multiplicity and flow pattern number are unexpectedly correlated, suggesting flow pattern fluctuations are a pertinent indicator of the thermalization time and viscosity of this dynamic. Furthermore, we discovered that final state multiplicity and flow pattern number are closely related in both LHC and lower-energy RHRA and RHIC experiments, with the difference in flow pattern number relatedness at top energy LHC revealing a notable increase in flow pattern time correlation.

We build upon a previous study to provide an alternative proof for the computability of first-order correspondents to (D)LE-formulas, utilizing ALBA algorithm techniques. Furthermore, we extend the computation of these correspondents to SA-formulas, and demonstrate that both computations can be performed efficiently, with a time complexity of $O(p^2)$, where $p$ denotes the number of variables in the given SA/(D)LE-formula.

This paper explores query answering in databases with incomplete information, particularly in conjunctive queries with disjunctions. We propose a new four-valued logic framework to handle information that can be both confirmed and conflicted. By applying the Four-valued Semantics of Davis-Putnam approach, we analyze and compute the true and undefined values of queries based on confirmed, conflicted, and impossible data. Our theoretical findings demonstrate that the true and undefined values can be computed by reducing the original database to two 3ACQs, each with potentially different sets of atoms. To further enhance efficiency, we introduce an algorithm that determines whether the resulting 3ACQs are equivalent and can be reduced to a single, simpler query.

We developed a novel linear line model, the Time-Varying Poisson AutoRegressive with eXogenous covariates (TV-PARX) model, capable of capturing complex nonlinear time-dependent dynamics and unit shocks in time series, including those resulting from sudden changes in external coefficients, data collected on a daily basis, and spikes in data recorded on a minute-by-minute basis. A Generalized Method of Moments estimator was derived and proven to consistently converge to its target value. To address the challenges of frequent parameter updates associated with real-world applications, we proposed an efficient recursive gradient-based estimation method. Furthermore, we demonstrated and formulated the relationship between the naive Bayesian approach and the TV-PARX model, enabling the incorporation of unit shocks into the Generalized Method of Moments estimator. Our findings indicate that the TV-PARX model and its associated recursive estimator outperform alternative approach in terms of both accuracy and computational efficiency.

Rigorous training of robotic handlers to process package contents is impeded by the sheer number of demonstrations required. In contrast, a single demonstration is typically sufficient for human learning. This study introduces Neural Descriptor Fields (NDF), a navigation framework that requires only a minimal number of demonstrations to navigate through envelopes with complex three-dimensional structures. NDF achieves this by encoding up to three layers of spatial information: two two-dimensional surfaces and a three-dimensional volume. By incorporating this multi-dimensional approach, NDF is capable of representing the user and the handler in real-time, even as they move. Furthermore, it can accurately handle the intricate relative positions between these components. By integrating this descriptive system with a method for combining features, we are able to develop a system that can process package structures with real-world complexity. Notably, NDF is able to navigate through an envelope with cylindrical structures and process mail from them, despite requiring a total of less than a minute of demonstrations.

The SiD Detector is a conceptual device designed to operate with the next-generation International Linear Collider. We have simulated the calorimeter and muon system of the SiD Detector using GEANT4 to verify the provided resolution data. The muon system employs G4MuonSystem v211b (21/11/2010), a revised version of the SiD's official muon system geometry as of 21 November 2010, which incorporates some recent updates to the system's radial geometry and material composition. The calibrated response of the SiD's calorimeters and muon system has been found to match the specified response values. Calculated and predicted muon system efficiencies exhibit only minimal discrepancies, primarily due to differences in algorithm usage. The computed resolutions for the calculated and simulated systems exhibit slight variations from the provided values in the SiD's official documentation, with calculated values for jet energy resolution exhibiting significant deviations below 50 Ge, likely resulting from modifications to the default jet algorithm used in the documentation.

We have analyzed the spectral features of three high-metallicity globular clusters,
including a newly discovered one named Tononzintla 2. Using the APOGEE-2
spectral data, we analyzed the metallicity and the dispersion in the abundance of
various elements such as alpha, iron-group, and others in each cluster.
We found that Tononzintla 2 displays a notable deviation from typical trends,
with a significantly higher spread in the elemental abundance (-0.42 $\pm$ 0.02
$[Mg/Fe]$ $\sigma$) compared to the other two clusters which have a much lower
spread (around 0.15 $[Mg/Fe]$ $\sigma$). This suggests that Tononzintla 2 may have
experienced a different historical process, with on-going star formation that has
different chemical properties in various parts of the cluster. We also observed
that Tononzintla 2 has a significantly higher metallicity and a lower central
concentration in the metallicity distribution than the other two clusters. A future
in-depth study with a large sample is necessary to confirm or refute this
hypothesis.

We have compiled the largest-ever dataset on the structural dynamics of formal proof repositories through an automated analysis of their dependency graphs, consisting of 15,846 proofs in the Isabelle/Isar archive. Our findings reveal that the node in-degree follows a scale-free pattern, while the node out-degree and edge weight distributions fit a power-law and exponential model, respectively. A further automated assessment has identified the core contributors within the archive and mapped their areas of specialization, showing the presence of distinct, interconnected clusters representing various subdomains of mathematics and computer science. The generated specialisation map for the Archive reflects the previously identified domains of key contributors such as Urbanic and Woltzenlogel.

The possibility of a confining deconfining phase transition in QCD at zero temperature and finite b-field is investigated, with critical deconfining debye radius $z_c$ as a function of deconfining parameter $\gamma$, de Haas van Alphen parameter $x$ and color charge $g$ for different values of $N$. For $N=4$, a distinct shift from the $z_c$ value of 1/3 is observed, corresponding to a $1/\sqrt{x}$ behavior, with $x$ representing de Haas van Alphen parameter, for $0 \le \gamma \le 1$. At $\gamma=1$, $z_c$ becomes 5/9, with future work planned to examine the phase structure in deconfining debye space, in addition to b-field and x. All of this is within the context of QCD in three dimensions.

This study explores the connection between the Tetration-Approximation-Policy (TAP) free energy and the convergence of the approximate message passing algorithm for a $\mathbb{Z}_2$-synchronization task associated with an arbitrary spectrum of the generator matrix. To ad-dress this, we derive a detailed form of the TAP free energy and demonstrate that its stationary points accurately reflect the exact overlap distribution. Furthermore, we utilize this result to simplify the original, complex expression of the TAP free energy.

The GSTC-based method has been successfully used for creating compact and efficient metasurfaces. However, limited research exists on applying the Generalized Sheet Transition Conditions (GSTCs) to accurately model highly coupled and three-dimensional microwave devices. This paper presents a new gstc-based approach for designing complex planar devices, incorporating resonant volume elements. By deriving an equivalent circuit circuit from the GSTCs, the method enables the precise characterization of these devices, including their surface scattering parameters and transferable impedance characteristics. This approach was validated using a planar horn waveguide device, demonstrating a derived circuit that closely matched measured S-parameters and transfer impedances. The proposed method offers a design framework for complex planar devices with reduced 3-D full-wave simulations, focusing on areas of interest.

In this study, we employ the blowing-up technique to modify coordinates and apply this method to support a proof of local orbital linearization for families of vector fields, specifically those exhibiting nondegenerate singularities. Furthermore, we provide a detailed analysis of how this coordinate modification impacts orbital linearization.

We've developed an ultra-fast way to test the efficiency of electronic structures generated by the eCPNN model. This method uses a modified version of the multiple-walker algorithm, called worm Monte Carlo, to check the accuracy of the wavefunction through an imaginary-time simulation. The process is done in parallel on regularized Monte-Carlo measurements, where our new way to sample the configuration using the eCPNN model allows us to check the electronic structure in its full form. This new technique, called 'deterministic collapse', involves the use of a set of pre-trained functions to generate a potential function that takes into account the interactions between electrons. Our new way to check the result is highly efficient and allows us to get accurate answers in a very short amount of time, with the answers matching known values for the Holstein-Hubbard model within a tiny margin of error. With this method, we can check the accuracy of the results for a wide range of conditions and the system size, with the new algorithm providing a margin of error of less than 1% for most conditions.

Recently, using two-year data from the Kepler Telescope, we identified a significant pattern in the star-planet frequencies it monitored. This anomaly appears to be linked to the moving window of Kepler's field as the Earth orbits the Sun. Although initially concerning, this finding can help refine the selection of stars Kepler could have surveyed more thoroughly if it had continued for more than two years. When analyzing the full Keplervallia structure in a three-dimensional map, the anomaly starts and ends with regions that seem to have no missing data. By applying a parabolic approach to predict where Kepler would have surveyed the most extensively, we found this optimal region to be about 1.5 times larger than what was actually observed, and oriented perpendicular to Keplia's long axis. This finding is crucial in determining which scientific questions Kepler could have answered had it never run out of time.

A new finding from wide-area photometry on wide-area cameras is demonstrated, showing that they can accurately measure the change in brightness caused by the atmosphere's aerosols over large areas without the need for precise calibration. As a result, even inexpensive cameras can contribute to monitoring the atmosphere's composition over wide areas. A previously reported observation from such a camera is presented, showing that the size of the atmosphere's particulate layer can be measured over large distances. Further research is required to confirm the general applicability of this discovery.

In estimating object pose in challenging scenes, our approach incorporates a prior knowledge of the object's appearance and symmetry by leveraging projection groupings of relevant and irrelevant features. By analyzing these groupings, we can derive a pose hypothesis that aligns with the object's symmetry and a visual metric that quantifies how well the grouping matches with the actual object in the image. This estimation is achieved through a projection-based neural network that analyzes a sequence of relevant and matching score maps to produce a symmetry-aware hypothesis.

In this theory, the peridynamic kernel's inherent disruptions are linked to the formation and location of fractures. This connection allows us to interpret the peridynamic prediction of fractures as an outcome governed by the kernel's structure. To proceed, the framework establishes the condition that the kinetic energy and the energy of stresses must remain consistent across the two systems. Furthermore, the framework defines the distance at which the non-local stress system simulates local stresses through an inverse of the peridynamic kernel. The study shows that the position of fractures predicted by peridynamics can be viewed through this simulating stress system and derives this predicted crack location as a stationary point of an energy functional involving the stress consistency condition. The framework also presents a numerical approach using this functional and provides an example of a material with linear elasticity to support this theory.
A new GGLX variant of Graphical Lasso is proposed, now accommodating hidden variables while estimatng the Maximum Likelihood for Gaussian variables.

To evaluate and compare various advances in Accelerated Molecular Dynamics (AMD), our study utilizes the alanine dipeptide as a test case and runs simulations through the ALAMODE package in parallel on a GPU using the KOKKOS framework. By modifying the original implementation of the AMD method, the ALAMODE package, labeled ALAMODE-AMD, offers the capability to assess and contrast the performance of distinct AMD methods. By incorporating ALAMODE-AMD with multiple ALAMODE force fields, we found that specific combinations, like the combination of the cold-spring Hamiltonian and the Reyton-Kroger resampling technique, offer up to a 10-fold speedup and reduce computation time by 50 percent and 70 percent, resulting in significant computational efficiency gains, including reduced computation time by 50 percent and 70 percent, resulting in at least an 11-fold speedup, reducing computation time by at least an 11-fold, reducing computation time by at least an 11-fold, reducing computation time by at least an 11-fold, reducing computation time by at least an 11-fold, reducing computation time by at least an 11-fold, reducing computation time by at least an 11-fold, reducing computation time by at least an 11-fold, reducing computation time by at least an 11-fold, reducing computation time by at least an 11-fold, reducing computation time by at

A comprehensive set of binary black hole movement patterns, involving the movement of a black hole pair through a gaseous environment, is assembled by using a numerical model that simultaneously solves Einstein's field equations and the equations of fluid dynamics with a radiative model. This scalardynamicsapproach, while not accounting for black hole spin, is capable of describing binaries of any configuration, including those with a surrounding disc, and is as follows: for a wide range of initial conditions, including a binary pair located at the center of a symmetrical, radiatively active accretion disc, its gravitational waves are accurately predicted, and for a binary pair situated near a quasar, its electromagnetic signals, such as those produced by the interaction with the surrounding environment, are modeled.

This research investigates the long-term behavior of a damped wave equation defined on a star-shaped metric graph with an infinite number of branches. elasticity were investigated in the context of this graph and their impact on the system's exponential stability was compared. The study revealed that elasticity plays a crucial role in determining the system's stability, and in graphs with an infinite number of branches, it was found that the system exhibits two distinct stability behaviors depending on the elasticity and Young's modulus along each branch. Specifically, the system exhibited stable behavior when elasticity was infinite, and unstable behavior when elasticity was finite. The proof of the unstable case was completed using a discrete model and a contour integral, and an alternative approach was proposed to complete the proof of the exponentially stable case.

This research Stycast 1090SI's acoustic characteristics in relation to PMMA were examined to determine the material's suitability as an alternative to PMMA. Testing involved measuring transmission and scattering of 1-MHz and 2-MHz acoustic signals through various Stycast 1090SI and PMMA samples. Results showed good consistency in the tests, with Stycast 1090SI exhibiting lower impedance and attenuation than PMMA at both frequencies. Although the material's thermoplastic nature leads to thermal expansion affecting its acoustic properties, Stycast 1090SI demonstrates comparable to slightly improved performance relative to PMMA, making it a viable alternative.

In this study, we examine how nodes and connections are ranked within multilayer networks that have varying layers, particularly focusing on the relationship between layers. To achieve this, we modify the betweenness centrality method to account for multiple layers and then assess different measures of connectivity within each layer. As a result, we obtain a comprehensive score that considers the significance of each node within its respective layer. However, calculating node importance within a single layer can be time-consuming for large networks. To tackle this issue, we develop an efficient algorithm to mitigate the computational burden by factoring in the network's multilayer structure. Furthermore, we examine how varying the relationship between layers affects the centrality calculations. Our method enables us to compare the results with existing betweenness centrality algorithms and reveals that linking a network to additional layers can increase the betweenness values of its nodes and edges. To better capture the inter-layer dependencies, we propose computing shortest paths separately for each layer rather than treating the network as an aggregate. Additionally, we introduce an adaptive policy to calculate shortest paths across different layers. This approach is formulated to minimize total computation time and is practical to implement. As the primary goal of our research was addressing computational efficiency, we did not alter the definition of betweenness centrality for multilayer networks. Nevertheless, we explore how different betweenness definitions influence the centrality calculations within each layer. To demonstrate the utility of our findings, we apply our multilayer betweenness centrality algorithm to real-world

We developed a novel, color-dependent point spread function (PSF) model for digital cameras, addressing the limitations of previous, monochromatic models. Unlike conventional models, our color-dependent approach accounts for the varying sensitivities of a camera's red, green, and blue filters. The model is complemented by an efficiency map that reflects the camera's reduced sensitivity to peripheral light. Together, they provide a comprehensive solution for accurately predicting the blurred appearance of point sources in images, considering factors such as location and brightness. The solution is implemented in a high-performance C++ program, executed on a graphics processing unit (GPU), enabling the efficient generation of realistic camera simulations.

The structure of the spinor representation for the Dirac equation in the R-minkowski spacetime has been thoroughly examined and the details of this representation have been x-rayed. The process of deriving the explicit form of the Dirac equation in the R-minkowski spacetime from the equation in de Sitter spacetime through a limiting procedure was also carried out. Furthermore, a thorough comparison was made between photon and electron spin in the R-minkowski and de Sitter spacetimes.

Structural Causal Models (SCMs) serve as a highly versatile and general framework for causal inference, offering a quantitative and mathematically rigorous way to graphically depict and analyze complex relationships, both temporally ordered and simultaneous. The 'cdt' package in R is a user-friendly tool for estimating and working with causal graphs, allowing users to create graphs that incorporate conditional relationships, both ordered and simultaneous, through both an intuitive interface and comprehensive subroutines. Implementing the methods outlined in Nadeau's thesis, the package allows users to transform observed data into a SCM, by deriving interventions, both observational and experimental, as well as calculating natural quantities, such as the Idoymica-Peres-Rosen bounds, to better inform causal inference.

A type of surface seal, known as an elastohydrodynamic contact, is used to pump liquids and gases at high pressures. Before failure, the pressure inside the seal's central area drops significantly, which may cause vibrations. To study this phenomenon, an experimental apparatus was built with a high-speed camera to capture the movements of the seal. Although the setup has limitations, it provides valuable insights into the expected behavior. Results show a direct correlation between the increased impact speed and the amplitude of the pressure-induced oscillations. To prevent instability, the difference in the impact's forward and reverse speeds must be minimal. As such, the rotation speed of the rotating component must be slowly varied, with less than 5% difference in both directions. If these precautions are not followed, the fragile equilibrium may be disrupted, causing the seal to collapse.

A recent investigation into the stability of vacuums in quantum gravity has uncovered a link between the existence of charged states and their masses. This study found that by manipulating the charge of scalarly unstable states, one could induce a generalized Witten effect, thereby rendering the vacuum stable. The present work deepens this connection between charged states and the vacuum's stability. It shows that the generalized Witten effect, in fact, governs the lowest-lying charged states' behavior. Specifically, an arbitrarily small increase in charge from the electric unit leads to a substantial rise in the associated excited states' masses. This threshold effect is surprising and has the potential to be utilized in model building involving scalarly stable de Sitter (dS) or anti-de Sitter (AdS) gravities. The potential application of this finding also suggests a possible extension of swampland conjectures to include anti-swampland thresholds.

Mobile applications are frequently targeted by malicious actors, and sometimes the vulnerabilities discovered allow for significant security breaches, as seen in the case of WhatsApp. To address this issue, a new framework called OctopOS has been developed, allowing for enforcing complex app-specific security policies post-compromise. Based on a modified version of Android, OctopOS utilizes a centralized policy manager to modify app behavior, inter-app communication, and system call processing in order to protect applications and prevent data exfiltration. A key feature of OctopOS is its modularity, allowing for easy extension with new policies, and its ability to operate transparently without requiring trusted components within the compromised applications themselves. Evaluation of OctopOS demonstrates its effectiveness in protecting multiple high-value applications, including Instagram, Snapchat, and WhatsApp.

We investigate the FPG algorithm under the assumption of subgaussian corruption within the context of episodic constrained Markov decision processes (CMDPs). The study aims to address the issue of episodes that may be compromised, where the states and rewards remain reliable, but the rewards and states in the policies may be distorted. We present a novel analysis that provides a guarantee of almost policy optimality under the Filtered Policy Gradient (FPG) algorithm, even when episodes are corrupted. Moreover, we demonstrate that the FPG algorithm achieves policy optimality without needing to assume bounded corruption. A key innovation in our approach is a new technique for analyzing the bias of value function estimates through the introduction of a projection operator that accounts for the corruption. Furthermore, we establish an exponential convergence rate for the FPG algorithm, even under conditions of corrupted states and rewards, as opposed to prior linear convergence results under pristine circumstances.

A solution to the original paradox of the "Two Envelopes" problem will be provided by element of choice concept, which pertains to an action that results in an identifiable difference between two options. Action that results in an increase of a quantity by an odd value is confirmed to be action of choice and has confirmed to have no impact on average value and also applies to quantization. Action that results in an increase of a quantity by an even value is proven to be action which is not a action of choice and has no influence on average value. Solution to the original"Two Envelopes" problem will be provided and also will be provided to an altered "Two Envelopes" paradox.

To address issues with mean-field theories that don't account for dynamic electron correlations, we used the dynamical mean-field + first-principles approach to model the cubanite mineral. This modeling enabled us to discover the energy range where the electron configuration is robust and exhibits unique stability and induced spin alignment. Moreover, we determined a magnetic threshold where ferromagnetism gives way to cantited magnetism. These findings were verified using experimental data on neutron scattering and X-ray scattering at energy levels above the dynamic correlation-enforced stable region. However, the transition between these regions enforces magnetic order by correlating the movement of localized electrons with that of itinerant electrons.

The study combines a quantum dot and an acoustic cavity to create a mixed spin-motion system, utilizing an acoustic wave to manipulate the spin through a radio-frequency field. By leveraging this method, researchers can precisely control the rotation of the quantum dot's spin and introduce new capabilities for spin manipulation. The effectiveness of this process is influenced by a quantum backaction effect, which results from the interaction between the quantum dot and the acoustic wave. The strength of this effect can be modulated by adjusting the frequency of the driving laser. In cases where the quantum dot-labeled phonon interaction is strong, multiple quantum dot states become coupled due to a significant frequency shift induced by a single phonon. It is found that in such scenarios, a damped oscillation occurs, and the quantum dot can be driven into a state where the majority of its population resides in a state orthogonal to its ground state.

A comprehensive examination of the herringbone lattice Hamiltonian is initiated, 
focusing on the effects of a momentum breaking perturbation. By analyzing various 
implementations within the Harrison-Morey model, the latent versatility of this 
framework is revealed. It is shown that the lattice can exhibit both non-abelian 
and commutative spin connections, depending on the nature of the applied 
perturbation, even within the context of a relativistic model. The equivalence of 
the non-relativistic and relativistic spin connections achieved, modifications to 
the spin connection in the non-relativistic limit are explored, and proposals for 
experimental realization using ultracold atoms on a suitably modified triangular optical lattice are discussed.

This study explores the use of single-photon catalyzed coherent states (SPCCSs), a type of non-Gaussian state that can be created by adding a single photon to a coherent state through either beam splitters or parametric amplifiers. Although these two methods result in the same SPCCS, they differ in their success probabilities, which depend on the device used. These success probabilities, essentially the inverse factorials of a parameter $n$, represent the likelihood of a specific outcome occurring, which can also be viewed as the maximum possible success probabilities, as lower probabilities may occur due to imperfect devices. Since higher $n$ values are less probable, SPCCSs with larger photon numbers are harder to generate. Consequently, comparing the average photon numbers and entropies of the generated states for the two methods reveals that the device with higher transmissivity, in this case the parametric amplifier with higher gain, has a greater chance of producing states with larger photon numbers and more entropy. However, in both cases, the distribution of probabilities follows a bell-shaped curve, rendering the states with larger $n$ values, which are crucial for some applications, relatively rare and thus entangled.

The Newman-Penrose formalism is a set of tools based on the geometric properties of null vectors that are well-suited for use with gravitational waves. These formats allow for a seamless transition from general relativity to the wave equation. Leveraging this advantage, the formalism is applied to a linearized approximation of the theory where gravitational waves are represented as a perturbation of the Minkowski metric. In this context, the complex coefficients of the Weyl tensor are expressed directly in terms of the gravitational wave amplitudes. Notably, only the $\Phi_0$ and $\Phi_2$ coefficients are non-zero in this representation. Furthermore, the Newman-Penrose extraction methods, which are based on these coefficients, are discussed within this framework.

A hypothesized polymer's electronic structure can be investigated through density functional theory, based on the arrangement of its constituent monomers. However, this approach becomes computationally prohibitive as the polymer's size increases. A new method has been proposed to infer properties of polymers with periodic defects, based on the collective interactions between its monomers. This method represents each polymer as a single entity, containing information about its periodic defect pattern. A corresponding energy function was defined and a recursive formula was developed to solve this function efficiently. The proposed method's advantages were demonstrated using a hypothetical one-dimensional periodic defect polymer and common polymerization forms. For these examples, method-derived properties were compared with theoretical and computational findings, showing a significant speed increase in computations while maintaining high accuracy.

This note makes the following key proof: It's possible to connect one ventilator to multiple patients and ensure they all receive the required air volume for ventilation. This is achieved by using parallel air passages with a branching design, specifically using a configuration where two patients are added through a 90-degree Y-piece. A crucial element of this setup is a bypass loop with an adjustable resistance, which can be used to control the air flow to each patient.

Accurate automatic segmentation of the esophagus from volumetric CT scans is hampered by limited and noisy data, necessitating enhancements to conventional methods. To address this, we developed a novel Deep Learning framework, the Dilated Dense Attention Unet, by integrating selective dense attention modules into an optimized Unet architecture. We implemented four attention modules with distinct designs to identify the most effective one. The framework was thoroughly tested using the public Radsys 2.0 dataset, yielding a total variation distance of 3.36, confirming its superior performance. The proposed method's effectiveness was further validated by a manual evaluation, demonstrating its enhanced performance compared to the baseline, and indicating its potential for a significant improvement in clinical applications by facilitating precise esophageal segmentation in volumetric CT scans.

Recent advances in horizontal multi-flow rate test logging and wireline measurements for fluid identification have made real-time formation evaluation feasible.
However, relying on traditional numerical reservoir simulation for this purpose is too slow to keep up with the real-time data.
We developed a novel lightweight model called a light reservoir moment model and created an automated optimization process to determine the logging parameters.
This allows for a more efficient and accurate formation evaluation through a new method we invented, known as Light Moment-based Evaluation with Reduced Measurement Logging (LM-EnRML).
Our results show that LM-EnRML takes less than a second to evaluate the formation, which is at least two orders of magnitude faster than the original analysis.
Additionally, we demonstrated the accuracy and speed of LM-EnRML through a field test, which confirmed that our method is reliable and efficient.

Our research focuses on improving named entity recognition (NER) by utilizing outside information, specifically low-resource corpus-level NER through the integration of text sections with the same entity type. A separate NER classifier is created for each entity type and these are combined to handle new texts. Our experiments on the OntoNotes dataset reveal that this approach yields the best overall F-score when dealing with nine entity types. Additionally, when entity types are categorized as binary decision tasks, the method outperforms traditional binary NER models on 13 out of 30 entity types. Notably, for entities with limited samples, such as locations and organizations, this model demonstrates significant enhancements with a significant statistical difference (p < 0.05).

We have developed an analytical method for studying the rationality of bitangents in a specific subclass of the Belyi parameter space of quartic curves with an anharmonic symmetry, where the anharmonic symmetry is fixed as the rotation by two units. By applying a tailored localization technique to reticulated models of the rational quartic, we have determined the rationality of bitangents in this parameter subclass through a detailed study of the tangent directions in a localized region, derived from the carvings of a specific hyperelliptic curve.

The proposed section presents a new algorithm for estimating the position of nodes in a network that rely on relative location data. This data is obtained by measuring angles between signals and comparing the results to an ideal algorithmic model. To achieve this, a simple maximum likelihood estimator is used. However, due to the non-Gaussian distribution of measurement errors, the estimator's performance varies, so a Bayesian framework is implemented to provide a more robust solution. Investigations into the algorithm's performance were conducted through simulation and a physical test setup, including comparisons to the classic triangulation method (15% average reduction in error) and a previously presented NLOS detection approach (10% average reduction in error), demonstrating the benefits of the proposed algorithm in locating network nodes.

Multilingual societies around the world have long been sources of both rich cultural diversity and intense conflict. To address these challenges effectively, it is crucial to develop cutting-edge natural language processing tools that can be accessed by a wider audience and solve real-world problems. Our research focuses on under-explored high-conflict multilingual societies, specifically on the Turkish-Azeri language pair. Through our presentation, we aim to equip researchers with the necessary resources to obtain the Educo 20k dataset, and also provide them with the opportunity to explore the Azeri education history. By leveraging the capabilities of modern NLP technologies and programming languages, we envision that Turkic NLP researchers and the broader community can gain deeper insights into the rich cultural heritage of Azerbaijan.

A significant number of existing image descriptions lack usability for the visually impaired community due to the absence of consistent best practices in their creation. Without established guidelines, current assessment methods for automatic image descriptions fail to accurately reflect their real-world usefulness. To bridge this gap, we present a preliminary framework for evaluating the accessibility of automatic image descriptions, complemented by a dataset featuring a diverse range of user feedback. We then utilize this feedback to refine the evaluation framework, proposing a set of accessible image descriptions guidelines that can be employed to guide and appraise the performance of automatic image description systems.

To comprehensively understand the complexity of local field, spin-orbit interactions within the computation of energy loss functions for the range of TaO materials, it's crucial, let's first examine the extreme cases where these factors cannot be neglected, specifically TaO and TaO2. Using first-principles methods combined with experimental validation, we found that ignoring these interactions results in a significant shift in peak positions and a marked decrease in peak intensity, leading to entirely different interpretations of the energy loss data.

A significant obstacle to understanding the online dissemination of fake news
is the inherent fragmentation of the internet, which is exacerbated by
geographical segregation. This research analyzes the online spread of
politically divisive information in China, a large market prone to
misinformation, and examines the impact of geographical segregation on
this dissemination. By integrating private survey data with public observations
from online platforms, we found that exposure to fake news varies widely among
different user groups and has significant implications for its dissemination.
Our analysis reveals that'The Big Sort' effect dominates, implying that users
who self-segregate from others on political issues are less likely to
share fake news. This phenomenon is further intensified among users who
reside in geographically segregated regions. The phenomenon is especially
pronounced among users who consume online news, which has significant
implications for its dissemination. This research provides a novel
quantitative assessment of the real-world dissemination of fake news among
different user groups, and our findings may guide the design of targeted
interventions to mitigate its effects.

This research aims to analyze how varying conditions during teaching tasks impact speech content. To investigate this, we used a large dataset consisting of 1042 video clips. These clips feature individuals with diverse backgrounds instructing others on assembling a kit set. By applying automatic speech recognition to the narration in the videos, we obtained text representations of the instructions. Subsequently, we used the Jaccard similarity measure to compare these text representations with each other and found that relatedness to the original instructor's background and related variables has a significant effect on the concepts conveyed in speech. This effect proved to be more impactful than other factors such as changes in demonstration methods. The obtained results have implications for areas including instruction learning from watching others, multi-agent instruction learning, and the design of learning experiences by watching others.

In our research, we've developed a novel algorithm for generating ordered trees based on specific degree constraints. The algorithm employs a dynamic programming approach, allowing for the efficient specification of constraints through a linear set of linear equations. Notably, it permits the independent definition of outdegrees for each node node type, outdegreeconstraisnt. The problem can be further solved in O(n) time, where n denotes the total node types, by applying a linearsystemsolver. The derived tree samples are ensured to comply with desired outdegree characteristics.

It has been previously demonstrated that finding the ground state of a quantum many-body system can be reduced to solving a set of Euler-Arnold equations. Building on this finding, we apply the approach to a quantum field theory within the functional Schrödinger picture. In this scenario, the system's configuration space forms an infinite-dimensional Grassmann manifold, and we derive the corresponding Euler-Arnold equations. These equations are then used to directly solve for the absolute ground state energy and wavefunction of the Hubble model, showing remarkable accuracy when compared to existing methods for the entire range of the mass parameter.

In the past two decades, advancements in machine learning have enabled the creation of sophisticated conversational systems that can seamlessly integrate into everyday life and various business processes. While these systems have gained significant popularity, the demand for quality assurance through automated testing has become crucial for their successful deployment. Unfortunately, the current testing frameworks available do not provide support for key aspects such as efficient test maintenance, automated test data generation, and integration with continuous development and testing cycles. To address these shortcomings, a new Python-based testing framework has been developed, offering quality assurance for machine learning-enabled conversational systems. This robust framework provides a modular structure for automated testing of complex systems, including features like efficient test maintenance, automated test data generation, and continuous development and testing cycle integration through tools like Jenkins. To showcase the quality and effectiveness of this framework, a real-world domain modeling assistant system was used for the demonstration, and its performance was evaluated, yielding a substantial improvement in BLEU scores of 17 points.

Researchers are using a unique approach with sensitive, wide-area sensors to find gravitational waves originating from interacting binary systems in nearby galaxies. By leveraging wide-field instruments and considering the limited angular resolution of gravitational waves, they can create a map of possible locations for these systems based on observed signals. However, to effectively use this approach, researchers first need to determine if there's an unknown object in the solar system about the size of Earth that could be generating gravitational waves. If such an object exists, its gravity would be detectable at a significant distance, specifically 38 Mpc, over 90% of the sky, according to full-sky analysis. Nevertheless, its wave signal would have to be extremely weak, with an amplitude of 10^-21, to have a measurable impact over most of the sky. Since current detectors like LIGO, Virgo, and KAGRA are more sensitive, even the smallest rocky moon would produce a detectable gravitational wave, although it may not be easily identifiable due to its broad probabilistic distribution. This research explores a cross-lingual memory retriever that dynamically selects relevant English sentences from multiple source languages to aid the translation process. The proposed model combines a monolingual encoder and a bidirectional encoder to translate sentences, and acquires bilingual pairs from two source languages. A contrastive learning module ensures the model favors matching pairs by maximizing their similarity. To evaluate the effectiveness, we conduct a few-shot experiment by training the model with 50 English-Japanese pairs and assessing it with 1,000 test sentences. The results show that the cross-lingual memory retriever improves translation accuracy by 12.44% over traditional Bilingual Translation Memory (BTM) models, and by 6.36% over monolingual encoders augmented with a attention-based Translation Memory (ATM).

This study applies the Liapunov center-manifold theory to analyze the dynamic behavior of the conformal Yamabe flow on the conformal metric defined within a domain of R^n. Specifically, it proves that fixed points of this flow correspond to constant sigma models. Additionally, the research shows that non-positive model values cause the associated conformal metrics to be eliminated under the flow. Conversely, within a specific local neighborhood of positive model values, it is observed that the associated conformal metrics will converge to their model counterparts as time progresses. Furthermore, the study achieves a notable breakthrough by providing the first analytical proof of the existence of time-periodic solutions to the time-dependent Yamabe equation on certain domains of R^3.

In few-shot learning, a common problem is the presence of outlier samples that can significantly affect learning performance. To tackle this, we introduce a novel framework for meta-learning with support sets, which dynamically identifies and extracts a quadratic subspace for each support set, effectively concentrating on the core task and pushing outliers into high-dimensional space. Theoretically, we can generalize from few support samples within this proposed model. The framework is adaptable and incorporates Riemannian manifold optimization for efficient optimization, support-relevant task features discovery using a task-gate network, and supports diverse loss functions. Experiments show that our framework achieves a 3.83% higher average accuracy than the second-best method on the CIFAR-FS dataset.

User preference is an essential element in recommendation systems, and rare positive interactions can significantly enhance the generalization of models. The Gated Aspect Preference Enhancement (GAPE) framework is introduced to incorporate aspect preferences into recommendations.  Within GAPE, two modules are used to integrate aspect preferences from both global and local perspectives.  Specifically, the Aspect Preference Enhancement (APE) module encolves aspect preferences into the main preference representation, while the Aspect Preference Gating (APG) module fuses aspect features with the user representation to produce an enhanced encoding of the user's preferences.  Notably, GAPE enables the leveraging of sparse aspect features to enrich the understanding of user preferences.  To further incorporate aspect preferences from both data sources, GAPE proposes the Training with Aspect Preference Enhancement (TAPE) strategy, which involves training objectives and a loss function that involve predicted and aspect-specific ranks.  Experimental evaluations on three public datasets show that GAPE achieves superior performance over 10 state-of-the-art recommendation models, and that TAPE leads to substantial improvements in the precision and recall of relevant recommendations.  Additionally, TAPE involves an increase of up to 30% in relevant and aspect-matching recommendations over analyses.  Additionally, case studies show that GAPE and TAPE involve improved performance.

This research focuses on nature-based formulations for integer programming, particularly Exotic Cones Integers (ECI) and Exotic Cones Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (ECMILP) models. These models integrate various Exotic Cones (EC) building blocks, including Big-M, rotated quadratic constraints (RQC), and minimum constraints (MIN), to model integer programs. We analyze the size and exogeneity of Exotic Cones within the extended exogenous formulation, and assess the exogenous and extended exogenous formulation performance using Exotic Cones exogenous (EC-ex) exogenous solvers from the Oracle of Exotic Cones Solvers (ORXCS) framework. Our experiments compare Exotic Cones extended formulations to standard extended formulations for MILP, showing the former offers a more intuitive and manageable model with reduced exogenous variables and Exotic Cones blocks, and that EC-ex exogenous solvers can outperform the Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP) solver the formulation was created with, and that they perform competitively with state-of-the-art extended formulations.

The data used to train and test machine learning models for medical image analysis has a major impact on their final performance. Overestimating a model's capabilities due to discrepancies between evaluation and training datasets can have costly consequences. To address this issue, researchers commonly employ cross-validation to minimize such risks. However, cross-validation is computationally expensive, especially for large datasets, making it impractical for many models and datasets. In contrast, a new approach called Risk-Aware Training takes a risk-sensitive subset of the training data, using it to train models evaluated on the remaining data. Experimental results show that this approach uses 10 times fewer data points than traditional methods while achieving 95% of the same performance. Furthermore, it excels over risk-map-based approaches and holds promise for replacing cross-validation in deep learning training.

We introduce a new framework for network-based optimization problems involving multiple agents, where the setup allows each agent to define its own local costs, which can then be combined into a larger network structure. The framework is used to define and analyze the decentralized feasibility problem, which is possible to solve using only local information within each part of the network. The framework is also applied to create a decentralized optimization problem, which is possible to solve through local gradient information within each agent's connected section of the network. The approach is illustrated with a case study of multi-robot feasibility and optimization problems, and general convergence properties are analyzed.

Researchers have investigated the performance of various optane DC PMM-based file systems for optimizing cached data caches, including the relaxed version of NOVA. In comprehensive benchmarks, NOVA outperformed other file systems, including the persistent LARC, showing up to a seven-fold speed increase for data within the memory cache and minimal gains for data not in the cache. To further optimize the cache, a new file system called FUSECT was created. FUSECT achieved similar performance improvements to LARC while reducing the overhead by a factor of three to four in writes when the cache was fully occupied. In comparisons, both FUSECT and the relaxed NOVA demonstrated significant gains in writes of up to three to four times the speed of LARC when the cache was fully occupied. Additionally, FUSECT exhibited better overall performance in benchmarks that involved mixed mixed performance.

Andrzej Kraszewski's research into the multi-agent motivation dynamics builds upon the original motivation dynamics model, which Andrzej developed and used to simulate various behavior patterns like exploration, routine formation, and risk assessment. In this work, Andrzej presents a framework where the motivation of each agent influences their actions in a specific way, leading to distinct action distributions that reflect exploration, routine formation, and risk assessment. This framework is an extension of the original model, which Andrzej applies in a multi-agent setting to simulate complex interaction behaviors, including rendezvous patterns that emerge from the motivation of each agent. In this work, Andrzej demonstrates how the framework can model simple and complex rendezvous patterns, including risk-based and motivation-driven interactions, and presents experimental results showing that the proposed model accurately reproduces these interaction patterns.

This study explores the effects of Cm and Gd substitution on the parent compound GdSn3's Gd $4f$-moment and hyperfine interaction. Using neutron diffraction and $\pm$13.5 nsec $\ ^{133}$Cs Mössbauer spectroscopy on the $^{115}$In resonance, the average Cm 5f-moment was also investigated in the $T < 0.2$ K temperature range for the samples Gd$_x$Cm$_{1-x}$Sn3, with $x = 0.75$, $0.625$, $0.5$, $0.375$, and $0.25$. The results from the Rietveld analysis of the data obtained from the three lowest temperatures of each neutron diffraction pattern, as well as the results from the Rietveld analysis of the corresponding $\ ^{133}$Cs shift and quadrupole splitting, are presented. The time evolution of hadrons, specifically quark-antiquark pairs like $qq\bar{q}$, within the Quark-Gluon Plasma (QGP) is intrinsically complex due to the various interactions at play. Heavy quarks experience color forces as they move through the medium, analogous to the strong interactions described by QCD, which also dictate how the quarks bind together to form hadrons. A novel approach is introduced to address the temporal dynamics of hadrons by integrating the real-time Schwinger-Keldysh formalism with the AdS/CFT correspondence, enabling the representation of hadrons as stable strings in a five-dimensional anti-de Sitter space. Within this framework, hadron formation is depicted through string dynamics, and we show that the hadron's velocity undergoes damping as it interacts with the plasma, consistent with both QCD and the AdS/CFT theories. Notably, the rate of hadron velocity damping is found to be related to the difference between the drag experienced by the quark and the anti-quark. The proposed model yields results for $B_{D_s^*} - B_D \approx 250$ MeV and hadron velocity damping $\gamma_{v} \approx 0.2$ GeV, derived from bottomonium data. These findings suggest that the model can be employed to study hadron dynamics in heavy ion collisions.

This work extends previous research on generalized patterns within the context of the symmetric group Sn to the Coxeter group Bn, incorporating the analysis of exchange laws and OGs standards. The study derives the exchange laws for the generalized standard OGS of Bn by referencing the generalized standard OGS of Sn, alongside a corresponding bijection between selected subsets of Bn and Sn. Furthermore, we provide Bn-specific formulas for Coxeter length and descent set based on the Coxeter length or descent set of the associated symmetric group element.

We have developed precise limits for the galactic halo properties of electric and magnetic fields, as well as a stream of virtual particles known as the dark matter annihilation flux. By combining stringent constraints from various sources of electromagnetic radiation, we have established the most comprehensive bounds to date. Specifically, we have used radio and microwave observations from different missions including WMAP, Planck, and GMRT to constrain these phenomena in the galactic halo. We have also discussed detection capabilities of the CMB polarization spectrum and the magnetic field's imprint on the far-infrared rotation measure (RM) to constrain these phenomena. We have also constrained the dark matter annihilation flux by leveraging an extensive database of infrared through gamma-ray observations of the galaxy. We have also discussed the potential for shrinking these constraints in the future with upcoming experiments such as the CMB-SCT, the CTHORRM, and the JWST.

This work extends the paring frame theory from $L^2$ spatial settings to frameworks of unique integrability for various spaces of conditional expected values. The theory is then applied to construct a stochastic integral within the dynamic paring framework.

The development of solid-state quantum technologies depends heavily on individual quantum emitters with consistent and easily understood properties. Research into a silicon carbide T centre ensemble shows a phenomenon called optical spectral diffusion with a time course that consists of two distinct periods - a short and long duration phase. Using an analysis of the charge carrier supply and the movement of the charge carrier cloud around the T centre, this research explains the optical stability seen at shorter distances and the moving boundary effect that causes the spectral diffusion's longer time phase at greater distances. It also highlights the impact of the T centre's size on its interaction with charge carriers and suggests that finding T centres with large diameters could improve their use in quantum applications by reducing the range of the optical stability.

This research paper examines two prominent approaches, Morphological Tools and the Region Growing Technique, for object detection in images. The study specifically focuses on tumor identification within images affected by a liver condition known as cirrhosis. The experiment was conducted to assess the efficacy of both methods. Results showed that the region growing technique offered more accurate tumor identification compared to morphological tools, exhibiting a lower error rate of 9.09%. In contrast, the circular formula approach exhibited a higher discrepancy, with errors reaching up to 45.45%.

In this study, we examine the degenerate Bernoulli numbers in depth. First, we establish their degenerate generating function. Next, we derive the degenerate Bernoulli numbers using both a Circulant matrix in $\mathbb{Z}_n$ and Galois fields. This allows us to obtain an explicit formula for the degenerate Bernoulli numbers. Finally, we prove the degenerate analog of Kummer's Theorem by leveraging the degenerate Crumpe-Lucas Theorem.

The ultimate goal of radial velocity (RV) research is to minimize measurement jitters to sensitively detect exoplanets with low masses. While various line list selection strategies have been explored to optimize signal extraction from noisy spectra, a novel approach is presented here. Instead of using predefined rules to choose lines, a randomized method is implemented where line sets are randomly generated within spectral constraints. These sets are then tested on available spectra to assess performance. The randomized method's output is evaluated against traditional line selection criteria across multiple spectra of three nearby stars that were used to calibrate the HARPS spectrograph for a decade. Although the average and minimal achievable RV measured by the randomized method slightly lags behind the traditional approach, its variability is significantly reduced, especially at its minimum values which are crucial for detecting small planets. Moreover, the variability of the randomized method exhibits less dependence on spectral signal-to-noise ratios. To assess the robustness of this strategy, a diverse range of randomly generated line lists were used to optimize the model. While all line lists significantly improved results over the default extraction and surpassed the performance of the hazel model, the optimal performance was achieved within the randomized method, where line lists were generated by chance. Hence, the study suggests that partially or completely randomizing line lists can optimize the extraction of RV data. Additionally, it is believed that the line lists generated by this strategy reflect physical interactions between electrons and atoms more closely, providing an implicit form of optimization.
