This analysis focuses on standard and marked ordered trees, specifically examining their deepest nodes in terms of the number of nodes overall. A key difference between these two types of trees lies in how their marked nodes connect to each other via edges forming cycles. This paper also incorporates matched trees, a variation of marked ordered trees, and discusses their asymptotic behavior as the overall number of nodes grows large.

Historically, elections have been secured through parchment and now through digital methods, yet character recognition through the process of optical character recognition remains consistent. This research aims to employ the character's written form as a reference to prevent vote alteration or tampering. To improve accuracy during the vote counting process using OCR, a spell-checking tool has been developed, following this model's definition on Google App Engine, and the experiment was conducted using the Tesseract engine, and the results were compared to using the Tesseract OCR alone. Consequently, the findings demonstrate that integrating the created spell-correction algorithm increased accuracy by 7 to 23 percent over using Tesseract without any correction.

When analyzing over-parameterized linear models with numerous time-dependent features, models often face an infinitely large data space. These features can be efficiently processed using time-sequential stochastic gradient descent. The model makes simultaneous updates across all features in each step, resulting in a model complexity that grows with the square of the total update steps. In the context of time-series data, this approach is inefficient due to its high computational demands. To overcome this challenge, a novel variance reduction technique has been developed, achieving the desired constant complexity in total update steps. This new method requires only a single matrix inversion during initialization and performs time-sequential updates, making it highly efficient and parallelizable in each step.

This study introduces a novel method for single-channel speech enhancement, building upon a directional attention mechanism by incorporating it in both forward and reverse directions in an auto-encoder structure. We specifically propose three models with bidirectional attention in different encoder-decoder components. These proposed models are also integrated into a deeper convolutional auto-encoder framework. Experimental results show that the model with bidirectional attention in the last decoder layer significantly outperforms other proposed models and various state-of-the-art speech enhancement methods. Furthermore, our proposed models demonstrate superior robustness when faced with high levels of background noise. All proposed models' codes and evaluations are made available on GitHub.

A new type of attack, the compromise pressure sensor attack (CSA), has been identified on Negative Pressure Rooms (NPRs). This occurs when the dual pressure sensors (DPSs) are manipulated by creating two separate openings, allowing air to flow in and out, effectively equalizing the pressure inside the room. To detect the CSA, we developed the CSA detector (CSD), a method utilizing the resistance measured by the DPS. The CSD can identify the CSA with high accuracy when the DPS's compensation mechanism is disabled. However, when the compensation mechanism is activated, the detection rate drops significantly, making it challenging to identify the CSA in many scenarios. A key insight has been that the CSA creates two separate flow paths, resulting in a discrepancy in the DPS reading that the DPS's built-in sensor cannot fully compensate for. Building on the CSD detection rate, a novel algorithm, the CSA identification module (CSIM), has been created to address CSA instances with low detection probabilities. The CSIM leverages the equalizer circuit within the DPS to idly detect the CSA and, when combined with the CSIM module, the CSA can be identified with a detection rate above 90%, with minimal impact on the DPS's normal operation, such as maintaining the negative pressure in the room.

The transition to low-carbon energy systems is being hindered by the potential for risk-averse energy storage to exacerbate carbon emissions during peak demand periods. Our study reveals that, depending on the flexibility of the energy system and the precision of carbon emissions forecasting, carbon emissions can increase by up to 50% in certain time intervals. Given this finding, policy measures promoting the adoption of risk-averse resources in the energy market need careful consideration. Our research model was applied to two energy systems and showed that, while generally leading to a later adoption of renewable energy, there is a risk of certain time intervals experiencing significantly higher carbon emissions. To avoid these negative effects, policy measures should be designed to promote the adoption of renewable energy even during peak demand periods.

The interaction of an x-ray pulse with a core-excited state, such as a core hole or an Rydberg state, drives coherent electron motion. This motion in turn modulates the transition dipole moment, affecting the absorption of subsequent x-ray photons. By using two optical pumps with different photon energies and a probe in a pump-pump-probe geometry, we demonstrate control of this modulation in argon. Pumping a core-excited Rydberg state with two ultrashort x-ray pulses induces significant shape resonances in the scattering continuum, reflecting the motion of an excited electron. The modulation of this motion by optical pump conditions was observed via a pump-pump dependent change in the x-ray absorption, providing a sensitive, all-optical diagnostic of electron dynamics. Notably, the spatial distribution of this motion is highly responsive to the transition energies of the two optical pumps in a regime where the Rydberg state is saturated. By modifying the x-ray photon energy of these pumps, we show how to tune the characteristic time scales of this spatial oscillation. These observations reveal the dynamic response of a multi-electron system to two simultaneous, ultrafast excitations and the influence of such dynamics on x-ray absorption.

Three-dimensional global general circulation models were employed to investigate a baroclinic storm on Mars, which occurred during the early northern hemisphere summer of the late Mars year 24. The simulations revealed that the planetary atmosphere's thickness influenced the circulation pattern, shifting from a two-layer system to a more differentiated atmosphere with distinct upper and lower circulation rings. The model accurately predicted the location and intensity of the storm, as well as the temperature and pressure anomalies within it. The development of the baroclinic ring current was triggered when the atmosphere transitioned from a two-layer to a differentiated circulation pattern, which was determined by the atmosphere's optical depth. The onset of the ring current was further delayed when the atmosphere experienced thermal inversion due to the heating of the lower atmosphere by the surface. This research utilized a sophisticated solar-thermal general circulation model that incorporated the effects of the Sun and heat from the surface on the atmosphere.

A primary aim of active learning is to minimize the number of labeled examples
required to achieve a specified level of accuracy. Effective methods exist for some
large-scale classification tasks using modest-sized datasets, such as ImageNet.
However, many of these approaches simply identify and obtain labels for the most
informative examples. As a result, they often yield poorly distributed labels,
which can hinder performance when applied to bigger datasets like ImageNet.
Existing active learning methods that aim to minimize variance and bias suffer from
disadvantages including slow speed and high memory requirements. In contrast, in this
study we propose an algorithm named BAL (Boosting Active Learning) that quickly and
efficiently generates the most active labels for all remaining examples in a single
pass. BAL delivers significantly more accurate outcomes than traditional active learning
algorithms on the ImageNet dataset and surpasses state-of-the-art variance and bias-
reduction methods. Moreover, BAL requires only linear time and constant space, and
can be integrated into standard classification pipelines.

This investigation builds upon the concept of algebraic multiplicity for matrices, which has been previously explored through the Schur-Jordan decomposition and recursive determinants, to introduce and characterize generalized algebraic multiplicity using the Schur operator.

To achieve quantum-enhanced sensing of an optical phase, utilizing two-mode squeezing is possible by combining it with a form of entanglement known as a cat state. Our proposal reduces the complexity of generating these complicated states by instead using the outputs of two independently created squeezed states as the basis for a form of measurement. This method results in the creation of a type of state with significant entanglement, which can provide a quantum-trailblazing level of sensitivity to changes in phase for its type. This type of state can be created relatively simply using currently available technology, and a form of measurement can be employed to achieve a quantum-level sensitivity in the desired application. This form of measurement is actually a simplified version of the type of measurement proposed to achieve the desired level of sensitivity in a previous form of cat-circuit quantum-enhanced sensing.

Researchers have been focusing on using electron spins in silicon to create mobile quantum processors, achieving significant milestones in controlling and connecting quantum bits. However, there's a challenge in applying uniform control electric fields to donor atoms at the nanometer scale due to location variations, which complicates the implementation of certain quantum gate types. To address this, a prototype PhontQ gate was developed using a 3D silicon structure to provide uniform voltage control and create a phase shift-dependent quantum gate operation. Using a variation of the Harris formula, this study demonstrates how to utilize and control donor atoms for a two-qubit gate, and presents a method to optimize the approach by separating the donor atoms, which also benefits error correction by reducing spontaneous error generation.

Resistive fluctuations near the lowest Landau level in substantial samples exhibit fluctuations with a macroscopic scale. This phenomenon was examined in a large n-type GaAs quantum well sample, exhibiting periodicity in a magnetic field applied perpendicular to the well. The two-dimensional electron density of the well was measured using the Hall resistance, and the resistive fluctuations were investigated by observing the resistive fluctuations of the well. A simple theoretical model was employed to calculate the fluctuations in resistance and obtained good agreements with the experimental results. It was found that the fluctuations in resistance are a direct consequence of scattering processes and not due to competing phases or topological defects. The calculations were based on the assumption that the two-dimensional electron system consists of a random potential and the scattering of carriers from the lattice.

This research proposes an innovative Adaptive Cooperative NOMA transmission protocol, which灵活ly adapts its strategy based on the availability of base station and base station access information at mobile terminals. Its objective is to maximize the system's overall performance while minimizing the likelihood of communication failure. A sophisticated, grid-based method is used to find the optimal solution efficiently. When the base station has access information, another approach, where the base station adjusts its transmission to support the user with poor channel conditions, is focused on. These two approaches are uniquely distinct from existing protocols, which are rigid in their performance and do not take into account the mobility of mobile terminals. Our proposed protocol, in contrast,灵活ly adapts its design to outperform existing methods and minimizes the risk of communication failure, while maintaining or improving system performance, as demonstrated through numerical analysis and experiments.

In dynamic Time Division Duplexing, the random fluctuations of spectrum direction, frequency allocation, and scheduling create significant challenges for coordinating uplink and downlink transmissions. This paper presents an optimal joint power allocation and scheduling strategy for dynamic TDD that minimizes total transmission power while respecting various spectrum-related constraints. A low-complexity, locally optimal solution method is also proposed to efficiently tackle this problem, and its performance is evaluated through extensive simulations, demonstrating, in particular, that scheduling strategies based on user statistics can substantially reduce signaling overhead and processing in real-world deployments.

We investigated a time-dependent model describing a heat-affected line moving through a type II superconductor with multiple vortex points. The model's parameters were carefully chosen to reflect the distinct properties of a line's resistance to the motion of vacancy defects (where the resistance to moving half a unit is less than the resistance to moving a single unit by itself). Focusing on stable equilibrium positions for a single vacancy and a solitary vortex, we derived and verified the long-term behavior of solutions to the model. Specifically, we found that a vacancy can become trapped in a local stability position, while a solitary vortex may move towards a wider stability position. The model's parameters were also explored in a report, and a diagram was provided to illustrate the conditions under which different behaviors occur. Notably, a vacancy may move towards a wider stability position if it starts with a sufficiently high initial kinetic energy.

A newly devised dynamic mean-field theory is evaluated numerically to obtain precise quantities for the Ising and Bloch-Heisenberg models under the influence of a magnetic field. This numerical assessment is executed across a range of temperatures and temperatures near the critical point, and it is done for multiple self-consistent algorithms. When a temperature-dependent relaxation time is incorporated, the algorithm including the finite magnetic field yields better agreement with known disordered-phase results compared to the algorithm ignoring this factor. A numerical analysis of cumulants, including normalized higher-order cumulants, provides a reliable method for determining critical temperatures and at no cost. It also offers insight into the impact of the magnetic field on the critical point's behavior, particularly in relation to normalized cumulatives. Near the critical temperature, normalized higher-order cumulatives display sensitivity to the magnetic field, and they show a pattern of convergence as the temperature moves further from the critical temperature. This theory further predicts that the critical exponents $\sigma$ and $\theta$ are both $1/3$, and this is confirmed through explicit calculation for the Ising model.

In 2D topological systems, the entanglement entropy of a state can be expressed as the difference between the von Neumann entropy of a spatial region and the rank of the corresponding matrix product operator. Notably, the term $\rho_A^\chi$ contains valuable information about the topological order, which can be linked to a set of 4-tensors known as correlation functions. Research has established relationships between $\rho_A^\chi$ and these correlation functions in specific topological models, such as the toric code, but generalizing this to all topological models remains an open question. Here, we prove that $\rho_A^\chi$ in such models is deeply connected to a set of 4-tensors that arise in studies of matrix product operators. These 4-tensors also appear in correlation functions, and for discrete-symmetry-breaking transitions, they offer new insights. Additionally, we investigate the entanglement entropy of a fundamental anyon in the Fibonacci model as a case study.

A Hamiltonian Neural Network (HNN) functions as a parametric estimator for a joint probability distribution, incorporating a specific structured constraint, which gives rise to a particular dynamic behavior. Leveraging this, we develop an incremental metaper learning algorithm that utilizes an MNIST dataset to train an classifier, representing both a joint distribution over data and parameters, as well as an implicit flow on a high-dimensional Hamiltonian phase space. Our proposed GFlowLSTM model outperforms a comparable LSTM-based meta learner with significantly less computational cost, which was striking considering the extensive storage requirements of the probability distribution compared to the LSTM, and also surpasses RNN-based few-shot learning baselines.

This research addresses a critical issue in deploying machine learning models by presenting a novel solution. Our proposed agent-based framework enhances a model's performance and reliability when deploying decisions. The framework employs two specialized agents called improvement and trust agents that collaborate to make optimal decisions. The improvement agent suggests an alternative class to achieve better outcomes, while the trust agent verifies if the main decision meets reliability requirements. Our experimental results show significant performance and accuracy improvements, with a minimal decrease in the trust score compared to a single agent, demonstrating the potential of our framework in addressing real-world challenges.

Recent advances in computer vision have been significantly fueled by large public
datasets,然而,敏感于公众情感的物品检测任务由于安全考量无法充分利用,
这一矛盾使得部分物品检测任务难以继续解决. 为了克服这一障碍,我们提出了
HiXray,一个新颖的行李X射线图像数据集,包含22种高危物品类别. 与传统的
物品检测任务不同,HiXray数据集的创建是出于安全考量,这促使我们设计了独特的
评估指标和实验方案. 利用这些方案,我们展示了即使是一个简单的卷积神经网络,
也能在相关且敏感的传感器数据中准确地进行高危物品检测.

Building on a recent framework developed by the author and K. Shumow, K. H. Ko is examining the polynomial invariant introduced by Cayley, which was originally defined for tree-labelled configurations, to understand the cases it can represent. To determine what kinds of links the invariant can describe, analysis involves studying how the polynomial changes in response to the R-matrix identity applying to adjacent vertices in the tree-labelled configurations. It has been found that $J_n^T$ does not yield invariants for virtual links but can produce both classical and virtual components when applied to weighted directed acyclic graphs.

A key issue in applying deep learning to tasks with limited labeled data is addressed by developing effective data augmentation strategies in NLP. Although numerous methods have been成功used, there's still room for improvement, particularly in designing efficient strategies for semantic similarity-based tasks. This research explores various data augmentation approaches, utilizes the Semantic Textual Similarity Dataset for testing, and compares different implementations, including those from the competitive STS 2019 competition. The experiment outcomes provide valuable insights, confirming that beneficial data augmentations can lead to significant performance enhancements, yielding more robust and efficient models. Moreover, the study offers a comprehensive framework for assessing data augmentation methods, facilitating future work in this field.

We build upon the innovative concept of complex representations of special functions by means of paths, specifically in relation to the Hankel path, which is used to define the Riemann zeta function and the Gamma function. This concept is essential to understanding the analytic continuation of these functions and their associated series or integrals. Combining the philosophy of the Hankel path with the series expansion of special functions found in the 'Special Functions' book, we have developed an extensive collection of new series representations for a wide array of special functions and identities, encompassing the most fundamental hypergeometric function $_2F_1$ and many of its derivatives, as well as the Bessel function, the incomplete Beta function, the incomplete Gamma function, the Airy function, the Whittaker function, the Legendre function, and more. Many of these complex representations are accompanied by descriptions of the paths used. Notably, the new series representations are derived through the manipulation of contour integrals and differential equations, both of which are key to the theory of special functions.

Top quark production is a key process in collisions at the LHC with sqrt(s) = 7 and 8 TeV. By combining data from these collisions, we measured a top quark pair production cross section of 266.3±5.5 (stat.) ±10.5 (syst.) ±12.8 (lumi.) pb, consistent with a theoretical prediction of perturbative quantum chromodynamics at next-to-next-to-leading order. Furthermore, we probed the existence of beyond-the-Standard-Model contributions by comparing the measured cross section to its confidence intervals with systematic and luminosity uncertainties to those of the standard model.

Our proposed framework predicts missing database contents and employs a predictive model to accelerate query execution in their absence. To verify its efficiency and reliability, we utilize a parallel processing system and an sequential implementation. The results demonstrate a up to $2.25\times$ increase in query processing speed on incomplete data sets, with no accuracy loss.

This paper introduces a novel analysis of privacy loss in graph-based machine learning, building upon the sensitivity concepts of neighborhood and interconnectivity. It addresses the limitations of existing analyses, which overlook the interconnectivity issue, by adapting the volume computation method used in the original DPS paper and incorporating it into the randomized response analysis. This results in a more precise computation of privacy loss in graph-structured learning than the current methods. The proposed analysis is also applicable to learning problems involving multiple graph neighborhoods. It involves a computation of volumes in the Grassmannian space, considering both the original and target neighborhoods. This introduces a new metric, graph sensitivity, which takes into account the interconnectivity of data points. The introduced computation method can be used in various settings, including the current model and the global model where a limited number of participants are allowed to modify a graph-based data set. The introduced computation method can be used in various settings, including the current model and the global model where a limited number of participants are allowed to modify a graph-based data set.

The Euclid mission, with a one-year lead time, is approaching and will have significant effects on a wide array of astronomical research areas. By utilizing the Euclid data analysis facility, eDAC, the expected outcomes include the following: refined analysis and perhaps the reconstruction of dark matter structures on the largest scales through the galaxy power spectrum and the galaxy-lens cross-correlation; the determination of Baryon Acoustic Oscillations through imaging and wide-field spectroscopy; the analysis of magnetic fields in objects such as the Milky Way, distant quasar hosts, and exoplanets using multi-wavelength datasets; the exploration of stellar populations and their relationships to the initial mass function using photometric observations in multiple wavelengths; the identification of rare objects through Euclid's enhanced sensitivity; atmospheric analysis of at least 100 exoplanets; a comprehensive survey of the X-ray sky with extended limits; a multi-wavelength survey of the entire sky in the far-infrared, helping to understand the history of massive stars and the development of supermassive black holes; the mapping of the Sun's magnetic field using photometry and polarimetry; atmospheric analysis using the Euclid fields; a survey of the Solar System; the identification of rare objects through Euclid's enhanced sensitivity; and the plotting of constellations for the northern hemisphere. This presentation will provide a summary of these research areas that will be discussed in detail by the scientific working groups during the Euclid workshops.

Accidents caused by the failure of automated lane keep systems on simple road
layouts are relatively common, primarily due to system bugs or incorrect sensor
data interpretation. Testing the reliability of the lane keep system in complex
road environments is a challenging task, as most road networks are already well
tested. To facilitate this, we've developed the RoadKeepEval framework, which
generates intricate road sceneries with numerous potential errors, including
misread sensor data, to test the lane keep system's performance. Using visual
simulators, we can test the system on a diverse range of roads and collect and
analyze test results. To make this process even more efficient, we have created
the RoadKeepEval-Benchmark dataset, consisting of 100k pre-configured road
environments with associated sensor and GPS data from real-world testing. This
dataset can be accessed at https://github.com/rke-lab/RoadKeepEval-Benchmark, and
the full document is available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.00370v1.

Developing a personalization system that accounts for user preferences and tastes
in various settings is increasingly necessary. Although numerous playlist
recommendation methods have been proposed, the potential impact of song lyrics and
metadata on the complexity of music catalogues has been largely ignored. In response,
this research aims to elevate the standard for music recommendations by proposing a
novel approach that incorporates audio content from tracks. Specifically, we present
a new model for building context-aware playlists, where the content of music tracks
plays a central role in modeling user preferences. To demonstrate the effectiveness
of our approach, we apply it to the Million Songs Dataset and conduct a comprehensive
set of evaluations, including a user study. Our findings highlight the superiority
of our context-based recommendation framework over existing baseline models, proving
its ability to deliver more relevant and tailored music recommendations.

Quantum correlations emerging from non-equilibrium quantum field dynamics hold significant interest, especially their classical counterparts, which may serve as prime probes of this phenomenon. Traditional approaches, such as the real-time Green's function method, often struggle with intricate quantum fluctuations, leading to an reliance on large-N or planar approximations. Here, we introduce a novel hybrid hydrodynamic framework, based on 3-point correlation functions, derived from the real-time Schwinger-Keldysh formalism. A linearized stochastic hydrodynamic scheme is then developed, which simplifies the problem by linearly stochasticizing the dynamics for a set of gradient-dependent quantum correlation functions. This hydrodynamic approach is found to provide more accurate results than holographic duality and large-N approximations, even at higher values of N, and is highly applicable to quantum field theories in any large-N context.

In this research, we focus on the task of action proposal segmentation, which
involves identifying and localizing potential action segments within a video. To
address this challenge, we introduce the Dual Context Aggregation Network (DCAN),
which is designed to create high-quality action proposals from a single video frame.
Our approach begins by extracting features from both the target video and a reference
playback, allowing for the modeling of temporal relationships between them. We then
employ a set of dense spatial predictors to generate feature maps for both the target
and reference frames. To capture global contextual information, we introduce an
aggregation network consisting of multiple modules that process these features.
Specifically, we use a graph construction module to build a spatial graph from the
target frame's features, which helps retain detailed information. We then utilize
reconnection and aggregation modules to integrate the reference frame's features,
resulting in enhanced, comprehensive feature representations. Our DCAN framework is
so effective that when used as a baseline, in combination with the Temporal Memory
Module (TMM) in the Temporal Action Networks v2 (TAN v2), it achieves the best
performance on the standard Memods and THUMOS-18 action proposal segmentation
benchmarks, improving the mean average precision (mAP) by 2.79% and 3.67%,
respectively. Our proposed network and the corresponding method for action proposal

In the context of high-confining-mode disruptions in the DIII-D tokamak, a specific type of post-disruption activity was observed, namely "supermodes." These manifest as palm tree structures in DIII-D chord-based emissive data and consist of localized edge modes surrounded by an internal island. A theoretical analysis using a two-fluid model reveals that they arise from the bifurcation of ELMs into an attached state and an island state, with the island state having a higher rotation rate than the attached state. The formation of PTMs requires the coexistence of mode numbers n=2 and n=3, where the inner island is associated with mode number n=3 and the outer ring with mode number n=2. The equilibrium between these two structures maintains the magnetic island's integrity. A real-time analysis of ELMs in a similar DIII-D plasma shows that the transition from supermodes to ELMs occurs via an inner mode number n=3 mode (island state) and that the magnetic island's rotation rate is indeed higher than the localized edge mode's rotation rate, aligning with observations.

A key challenge for autonomous mobile robots using potential field method navigation is avoiding obstacles in narrow passages. To address this, we propose an improved approach by incorporating repulsive potential field definition with vorticity. This method allows the robot to effectively avoid obstacles in tight spaces by creating an infinitely strong and rotationally balanced repulsive field. We analyze the velocity vector's behavior in relation to vorticity and identify optimal values for obstacle avoidance. Furthermore, we compare these ideal values with those traditionally used in potential field methods.

This study explores the application of the quenched large deviation principle for sequences of letters, specifically focusing on the probability of extended periods without a specified subsequence. By leveraging the principle, we derive an exponential law governing the longest occurrence of a renewal process, in accordance with tail distributions, within the domain of letter sequences.

This paper investigates the potential of using intelligent reflecting surfaces to compensate for obstructed or line-of-sight-free radar links. By analyzing the characteristics of the reflected waves, we derived a novel framework for radar detection that takes into consideration the intensive nature of channel statistics. Our findings demonstrate that IS surfaces significantly enhance the probability of detecting targets, particularly in scenarios without a direct line-of-sight. To quantify this improvement, a closed-form expression was derived, indicating an increase in detection probability of up to 500 percent. Furthermore, simulations reveal that radar performance also benefits from increases in reflecting surface area and incident signal power. We further explored the impact of IS surfaces on the ability to distinguish between targets with different reflection coefficients or direct-to-reflection coefficient ratios, and found that such capabilities could be distinguished with high accuracy (greater than 99 percent). This research underscores the promise of IS surfaces in extending the operational range and capabilities of radar systems.

Mutation analysis is a modern technique that evaluates and compares the effectiveness of fuzzers, enabling an in-depth analysis of program comprehension at a fine-grained level. By plugging into a fuzzer's internal components, including the fuzzer itself, this method provides the most comprehensive comparison to date, resulting in several mutation analysis techniques being developed and widely adopted in recent years. However, a key obstacle persists in program comprehension analysis, namely the difficulty in linking observed program behaviors to their underlying causes, particularly when multiple execution paths are affected by inputs and there are numerous program locations influenced by them. In order to overcome this challenge, we introduce EvalFu, a script-based mutation analysis tool that integrates with fuzzers, starting with Lufax, our high-performance fuzzer that builds upon ClamFu and achieves top performance in the ongoing Fuzzing Challenge. EvalFu targets both the input and internal states of programs under test, employing efficient algorithms for reachability analysis guided by mutation analysis, including the production of boolean, program-counter, path-sensitive, and value-sensitive guidance mutations. At the core of EvalFu lies a high-performance data structure, the efficient-frontend (efr), integrating with the evaluated program's memory to accelerate reachability analysis by up to 4 orders of magnitude, surpassing existing mutation analysis tools in both speed and effectiveness. EvalFu's superior performance is highlighted by comprehensive benchmarks consisting of 10 years' worth of entries in the DEF CON CTF and the Google Code In, along

Current research on matrix factorization-based continual learning often utilizes online factorization techniques, where new tasks are learned by updating latent factors in real-time. These methods start with uninitialized factors and achieve promising results. In contrast, we discover that using pre-trained models in matrix factorization-based continual learning is beneficial, yet existing models typically fail with this approach. Our investigation reveals that nearly all current matrix factorization-based continual learning algorithms suffer from catastrophic forgetting when given pre-trained factors. In response, we introduce an incremental nearest mean learning algorithm that secures the task boundaries of new categories relative to previous ones. This method can be applied repeatedly and, contrary to expectations, reveals that it uses online factorization techniques effectively. Our method brings several key advancements: we demonstrate that with pre-trained factors, the NMC surpasses state-of-the-art matrix factorization-based continual learning routes; we show that the NMC works well with both linear and non-linear models; and we find that the NMC exhibits superior performance compared to leading matrix factorization-based continual learning algorithms in non-linear settings.

For a given integer k greater than 1, a new concept is introduced: the higher, lower, and average thresholds associated with a specific integer k. It is demonstrated that the k-th homotopy group's triviality can be linked to the existence of a specific, limited set of obstacles from a group known as the trivialisability obstacles. Specifically, if the k-th homotopy group is already established as trivial, any maps that are n-dimensional can be modified without introducing the need for an infinite supply of those specific obstacles. Additionally, a new criterion is introduced: a map is considered (n,k)-connected if it matches a highly (k-dimensional) connected relationship between two wayfarings that are n-dimensionally connected. Under this framework, a limited set of formulae is given to identify when a particular type of map is (n,k)-connected, assuming that certain group extensions related to lower homotopy groups are non-trivial. As a consequence, a specific set of formulas is given to determine the extension of a single loop loop space along a specific set of obstacles if the start and end maps meet certain homotopy requirements and the relevant lower homotopy groups have already been established as having a specific, limited set of values.

We analyze a degenerate reaction-diffusion equation with a strongly degenerate diffusion term dependent on $u$, investigating the long-term behavior of solutions in a one-dimensional bounded domain. Our focus is on understanding how the equilibrium point's stability, one-time boundary values, and specific properties of the reaction function influence the asymptotic dynamics of solutions within $R^2$. We also examine cases where the stable equilibrium point is at the origin and where $f(0)=0$ but $(0,e_1)$ is the stable equilibrium. We also investigate the impact of the reaction function on the asymptotic behavior in $R$. We particularly note that in a semi-infinite strip, the equilibrium point reached at the origin may be stable only when $f(0) < 0$. We proved these findings through detailed analysis, including the use of a transformation to handle the degenerate term and the use of the comparison principle to establish the asymptotic behavior. We used this finding to identify the threshold behavior in a Bogdanov-Tikhonov normal form.

To properly examine the structure of the neutron subshell gap at N = 40 in the 64Ni nucleus, time-dependent shell models were employed. Timeslice energy surfaces, derived from multiple models of the shell model, and global observables such as energy parameters and alpha-particle binding energies and radii were compared and analyzed in detail. Starting with neutron single-particle energies, adjusted through configuration mixing and corrected for the proton core excitation via an effective interaction, we found that only a small subshell gap is to be expected in 64Ni. To further clarify this, we derived an effective gap size by subtracting the gap in a neutron analog state with filled d3/2 orbitals from the gap in the ground state. A small effective gap size of about 1.5 MeV was found, and its variation across different models correlated closely with the observed changes in the root-mean-square radius and the energy parameter $\delta W_{\alpha\alpha}$, and to a lesser extent, with the found variations in the matter radius and the alpha-particle binding energy. To deepen our understanding of the effective gap size, we related it to the effective monopole interaction between neutron d3/2 and f1p orbitals, and utilized the Large-Spacing Model to predict a negative value of about $-$2.5 MeV. In game theory, Lipschitz games limit how quickly a game's outcome can change in response to shifts in strategy, using a single value applicable to all players. This concept diverges from various, less widely studied definitions that specify different maximum rate-of-change values for each player. Our work builds upon a unified definition of strategy-dependent rate-of-change limits, encompassing both the broader and narrower definitions. Under this unified framework, we prove that optimal strategy combinations exist and can be found through a unified existence proof and computational method, applicable across all variations of this definition.

This study introduces the J-K Fold technique, a new cross-validation method that Jates in multiple runs with overlapping test sets against the standard K-fold approach. For instance, 5-K Fold encompasses 3 distinct test sets, each consisting of 20 percent of the data. Jates employed J-K Fold for tuneing hyperparameters in three deep learning models with over 10 million weights each. Notably, the author discovered that 5-K Fold yielded a 20 percent more accurate performance prediction than 10-K Fold. This implies that the J-K Fold technique results in less variable hyperparameter tuning and the technique also leads to more efficient computation as demonstrated by the experience of Jates.

Assistant Student-Teacher training techniques have been proven effective for creating efficient models, even when the teacher is a single high-capacity network. These methods have been utilized to develop a wide range of student models that excel at image recognition, natural language understanding, and other tasks. However, most research involves either extremely lightweight or very large teacher networks. Our study shows that a mid-range teacher, specifically one based on a Knowledge Distillation framework, has the capacity to produce superior results compared to both very light and very heavy teacher models. We demonstrate this by creating several knowledge-based teacher models and showing that they can be knowledge-reduced by means such as Logit Knowledge Projection (LKP), producing a family of teacher-student pairs that consistently beats comparable architecture-based models across various evaluation criteria.

In recent developments, learning exact methods of inference and optimization in Markov networks has seen a breakthrough, with Glielmo and Salakhutdinov's adaptation of bucket elimination demonstrating state-of-the-art performance on large, manually constructed datasets. Notably, this approach outperforms the currently leading approximate techniques, including BPG, contrastive divergence, and score propagation. Bucket elimination's capability to handle both optimization and inference consistently allows it to overcome the drawbacks of other methods, such as the bias and variance issues, and provides a more comprehensive solution by yielding an lower bound on the partition function, in accordance with the maximum likelihood objective, and updated marginal probabilities for each variable, such as the optimized parameter values.

The line shape formed by a light absorption peak at a atomic resonance shifts in high saturation levels, and our research reveals that the famous Stokes lineshape observed in such conditions results from an underappreciated effect: line narrowing caused by recoil from emitted photons, which becomes prominent in absorbers with low momentum transfer. Using a detailed theoretical model, we demonstrate how photon recoil influences lineshape in various contexts and offers a way to measure the two-photon transition width. In case of a low-velocity target, like a neutral atom in a optical molasses, this transition gives access to a fundamental property: the natural spread of velocities gained by the atom due to the random recoil from absorbed and re-emitted photons. This study also highlights the importance of considering the lineshape change on knowing the true transition frequency and reveals new approaches to minimize it through highly saturated interactions. As a result, we propose using highly saturated transitions as highly precise frequency references for optical clocks.

The critical exponents of the first-order disorder transition in granular mixtures, 
which experience both friction and repulsion, have been calculated using the 
Entropic Dynamic Quenched function of proper quantities, considering proper 
symmetries and the interplay of friction and repulsion, using proper 
characteristics of both the isotropic and shear-jammed states, and the results 
are verified through direct simulations.

The centralizer of the power D(n, x^2) within the special linear group Sln(x) has a central element Z(n). This element's centralizer has a centralizer with a Hilbert-Poincaré series that can be rewritten as a rational function. The rewrite can be represented as an infinite sum of terms, involving a finite number of components, where each component has a distinct Hilbert-Poincaré series. The proof relies on an inductive argument, with each step building on the previous, where a element from Special linear group Sln(x) has a redefined, central element, with a redefined, centralizer with a redefined, Hilbert-Poincaré series that can be rewritten, with a redefined, rational function.

The presence of weak interactions between neighboring spins, known as Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya (DM) interactions, can be influenced by applying a pressure-induced change in material structure, kosevich demonstrated. These stronger forces arise from specific materials and can now be regulated through mechanical strain. The research involves ferrimagnetic material GdFe$_2$O$_4$, whose spin structure consists of two layers with opposing spins separated by a magnetic anisotropy barrier created by DM interactions. Applying high pressure causes the spin structure to twist, overcomes the DM barrier, and results in a new magnetic state, known as the weak skyrmion lattice phase, characterized by a hybrid of two types of spiral orders. Sonics can detect this transition and the pressure can be adjusted using small devices, such as piezo actuators.

This letter discusses the detailed structure of a one-dimensional (1-D) WIMP velocity distribution, which is derived from the larger velocity distribution of the incoming halo WIMPs. We develop a set of formulas to describe the 1-D distribution in terms of the minimum and maximum velocities, which define the unique "slice" of the incoming WIMP velocities. These formulas hold true for any smooth function describing the overall velocity distribution of the incoming WIMP halo. We use both analytical and numerical techniques to derive and verify these equations. The results demonstrate distinct features in the 1-D distribution that correspond to the structure of the incident halo. For instance, the 1-D distribution exhibits an asymmetric shape, taking on an elliptical form at low velocities and transitioning to a parabolic form at higher velocities. Additionally, we discuss the impact of the halo structure on direct dark matter detection experiments.

The proliferation of online information has made searching for relevant data among vast quantities both necessary and complex. To facilitate this, search algorithms are employed, but the potential for bias in the results poses a risk of spreading misinformation and distorting perceptions of reality. For government professionals who rely on search engine results to perform their duties, this issue is even more pressing. To address this challenge, a study was conducted following an open data initiative, where a survey was administered to public sector employees in Israel. Additionally, researchers performed a lab experiment to better understand how these professionals are affected by the inherent biases in search results. The findings from both components of the study are presented in this paper.

A new point-spread function (PSF) is defined as the response to a point source,
which, according to energy conservation, equals the squared magnitude of the sampling
beam divided by its solid angle of incidence. This definition is termed 'natural'
as it adheres to fundamental conservation laws. In the rCASPR method, a different
definition of the PSF is used, leading to violations of this principle. To overcome
this limitation, simulations and experimental results with transmission-grating-based
sampling show that the rCASPR PSF retains symmetry and that the method enhances
image contrast while maintaining energy conservation. Additionally, the feasibility
of this approach is confirmed by sampling results that align with theoretical predictions.

This paper introduces a novel mathematical construct called nonnegative control Lyapunov and Control Barrier Function sublevel sets, abbreviated as ICCBFs, to address both safety and stability concerns in control systems that consider higher-order dynamics. ICCBFs can be utilized in a wide range of systems, including those that handle Higher Order Control Barrier Functions (HCBCFs) and Finsler Lyapunov functions. By deriving an ICCBF from the intersection of ICCBFs that represent individual HCBCFs and a Control Lyapunov Function (CLF), a single ICCBF is created whose sublevel sets incorporate both safety and performance information from the HCBCFs and the CLF. A control law based on a receding horizon approach, called the i-CCBF NCLF, is proposed to handle control systems that incorporate both Control Barrier Functions (CBFs) and Control Lyapunov Functions (CLFs). Simulation results are provided to validate the effectiveness of the i-CCBF NCLF in ensuring both safety and stability across various control systems.

In this research, we extend the concept of CF-applications between relational spaces, and investigate the properties of CF-closed sets within CF-approximation spaces, drawing a parallel to closed domains in relational topology. Our findings demonstrate that in CF-approximation spaces, CF-closed sets possess a Finiteness Condition and can be defined through local characteristics. Furthermore, we show that continuous mappings in CF-approximation spaces can be accurately described based on local behavior, and we establish a relationship between continuous functions and monotone mappings between CF-lattices.

We have developed an innovative exact algorithm for implementing Paired-Permutation Tests, leveraging a paired t-test and Monte Carlo simulation of paired permutation sums. The algorithm employs dynamic programming to efficiently compute the precise distribution of squared sums, allowing for an exact p-value calculation even with a relatively small initial Monte Carlo sample size. The paired p-value derived from this method can be multiplied by itself (or combined with another paired p-value through multiplication or Bonferroni adjustment) to address common p-value analysis scenarios. In tests, the new algorithm demonstrated remarkable speed, being 100 to 1000 times faster than repeatedly Monte Carlo sampling, particularly for a typical data set consisting of 20 to 30 features evaluated on approximately 200 to 300 instances. The algorithm's speed allows it to exactly compute p-values for paired permutation tests on practical-sized data sets within a short time frame, for example, for a data set with n = n' = 500, the p-value can be determined exactly in about 1 second.

A significant shift occurred in 1983 with the collapse of the International Maritime Bureau, a event that substantially impacted the global shipping industry by increasing competition. This study leverages unique data from New York freight prices to analyze how the decline of the bureau influenced the relationship between prices in New York and the rest of the world. The results demonstrate a marked decrease in the prevalence of monopolistic practices in shipping following the bureau's dissolution, with competition increasing by a ratio of 15 to 20 times. It's also crucial to note that the dissolution event provided a rare and valuable opportunity to study the impact of increased competition on prices, as it resulted from an uncompensated transfer of assets between parties, thereby preventing any distortion in the data. Although the increase in competition had a minimal effect on shipping quantities, it substantially impacted prices, with New York prices converging with world prices to a degree of 85 percent over a nine-year period. Furthermore, the impact of the bureau's dissolution on prices was found to be influenced by shipping distances and a variety of structural breaks, with other factors such as world productivity and oil prices playing a role. Ultimately, the findings demonstrate that increased competition in shipping significantly lowered prices, with a decrease of 15 to 20 percent, with a corresponding increase by 5 to 7 percent.

We have successfully proven the existence of a Gromov-metric-compatible $4$-dimensional PL-triangulation for every loom space of dimension two. This achievement involves the adaptation of Gromov's concept of polytopal complexes to the field of piecewise linear (PL) topology.

Recently, there's a growing interest in graph neural network research. A significant amount of work focuses on improving node representations by optimizing task-specific node features, often neglecting the graph structure's impact, assumed to be fixed. In comparison, node features are known to be easily optimizable, suggesting graph structure has greater inherent informative content. Based on this assumption, we propose a method to directly optimize graph structure, starting from a random initial structure. We introduce node features and a reinforcement learning algorithm with a task-related reward function to guide the evolution of the graph structure through node and edge addition/removal. Our method shows superior performance to node features optimization alone, allowing GNNs to achieve high accuracy with basic predecessors. Notably, our optimized graphs consistently exhibit clusters of nodes with similar labels, confirming the method's effectiveness. A detailed implementation is available at https://github.com/zhenghaofei/OptimalGraphStructure.

Adaptive one-sided listwise missing data, characterized by the absence of response values for certain data points, can influence traditional dimensionality reduction techniques that rely on average values or eigen-decompositions. Although learning robust models from such data is challenging due to the lack of missing labels, leveraging the known relationships between features and the response can help identify and exclude irrelevant or overemphasized eigen-directions. Although the exact relationships are typically unknown, they can often be approximated using simple regression models. Based on these approximations, various eigen-directions with different impacts, such as bias and variance, are identified and filtered using corresponding criteria using traditional eigen-decompositions. Notably, by applying the filter to input, known in the literature by the use of such a technique, leads to more robust directions and more effective performance using other traditional eigen-directions based methods, supported by the support of theoretical analysis and extensive experiments.

This paper compares various approaches to geometry and topology based on the behavior of certain minimal surfaces in a given space. By putting specific methods to test on a recently discovered object in Finsier 3-space, we can see how different style arguments yield comparable results to existing theoretical frameworks, particularly the Chern-Keating analysis.

A persistent question regarding the nature of a vortex in superconductors is whether it should be viewed as an individual entity or as a localized region of entangled normal electrons within the surrounding superconducting lattice. A vorticity field is introduced to address this issue and elucidated through a comparison with the entropy contained in the vortex core, which is found to be significantly lower than the motion-induced entropy of a moving magnetic flux line. This discrepancy is used to demonstrate the inadequacy of existing models that treat the vortex as a neutral carrier of a moving magnetic flux. Furthermore, new evidence suggests that an electron attempting to move as a flux carrier would experience massive electrical resistance due to the superconducting lattice's opposition.

This paper explores a noniterative communication approach for a centralized system that coordinates a vast number of independently controlled devices. We focus on a specific setup where a central unit (aggregator) makes adjustment suggestions based on system data received from among other things, with the aim of efficiently achieving a target frequency, and receiving feedback in return. We derive an analytical formula to calculate the optimal method for the aggregator to provide feedback, guided by principles of maximum uncertainty. We demonstrate that this approach results in a straightforward, non-recursive system response. We explore various scenarios to reveal the characteristics of this approach and its potential advantages over traditional methods. Finally, we simulate a grid system to validate the effectiveness of this approach.

This paper presents a novel deep learning approach that integrates machine learnable features, specifically technical indicators and previously predicted outputs, into a recurrent structure to anticipate stock movements. The proposed method's performance was tested using public stock data from the New York Stock Exchange, and results show that this approach can effectively predict the direction of stock movements. An alternative comparison using a basic probabilistic model confirmed the superiority of our deep learning framework. Furthermore, this study extends to the prediction of financial time series with complex patterns. The code and results are made available online for open access.

The sensitivity of the Large Synoptic Survey Telescope will be groundbreaking, allowing researchers to study the full range of supernova events. When white dwarfs merge, the outcome can be a type Ia supernova, a neutron star, or the complete disruption of the white dwarfs. In this study, we focus on type Ia supernovae produced by merging white dwarfs and how they will appear in the sample the LSSST will collect. We use recent findings from the Advanced LIGO gravitational wave detector to refine our predictions for these events, along with prior findings on finding such waves. The results we obtain are essential in shaping future research into binary white dwarf systems. To do this, we examine the events' recurrence rates, detection probabilities by the A.L.I.S.S. survey, and the likelihood of finding optical signatures prior to or during their collapse. We also explore the parameter space in which different outcomes occur and how this influences our predictions. Ultimately, these findings are crucial in determining which scenarios will be observed.

To address double Higgs boson production, we examine the relationships between the Higgs Effective Field Theory (HEFT) and the Standard Model EFT (SM EFT). By expanding the SM EFT around an HEFT equivalent, we determine the correlations between their respective higher-order coefficients. The double Higgs data lie within the overlap of the validity ranges for both EFTs, implying that such analyses are compatible. Furthermore, based on these similarities, we propose using a hybrid effective field, the "fat Higgs effective field" (fHEFT), where the s-channel amplitudes adhere to the SM EFT, while t-channel aspects follow the full HEFT. Notably, the v2 channel, often treated as part of the SM, exhibits large differences between the two theories, potentially offering a distinguishing feature for the two models. The advantages of the fHEFT approach over the existing EFT frameworks are highlighted.

In our approach, we establish a framework for a framework that can be considered 'pre-non-relativistic' and use it to enable an analytical expansion in general relativity. This framework sets the time coordinate based on the flow of a slow velocity field and results in the time derivative being 'pre-non-relativistic'. By implementing this framework, we can perform an analytical expansion of the Einstein equations in terms of the slow velocity, providing a framework for post-Newtonian expansions within this framework. This framework simplifies the post-Newtonian expansion in the P gauge and enables the use of a weak field approximation to obtain a further simplification, resulting in the post-Coulombian expansion.

We revisit the holographic renormalization process for $k$-th order theories, using VSIR based methods, and demonstrate its connection to the canonical formalism of HRe, which also at the $k$-th order, is analogous to the recent findings of de Haro, Skenderis, and Soler. As an illustration, we examine the $k=2$ case, corresponding to Einstein gravity, in detail. By dividing the Einstein equations into two first-order equations, we find that the combined subdeterminants of the full matrix used in the VSIR method accurately represent the expected 1-loop holographic effective action. This leads to a more intuitive understanding of the deharmonic counterterms in the VSIR approach. Furthermore, our computation of deharmonic counterterms aligns with the computationally more feasible procedure of adding local heat kernel counterterms, particularly for near-boundary expansions with smooth sources, as smoothness is not always guaranteed, as seen in the case of compact manifolds. This near-boundary smoothness issue has significant implications for the computation of 1-loop determinants.

We investigated the motion of a horizontally moving cylindrical intruder in three-dimensional simulations of two-dimensional granular beds, which are simulated using the discrete element method. The cylinder's driving rate was varied, and its effect on the drag force was studied. The simulations showed that the cylinder induces an asymmetric flow in the bed, which results in a significant inertial drag force that dominates over friction-related drag. This asymmetry arises from the differences in relative velocity between the cylinder and the bed's boundaries. As the driving rate decreases, the flow pattern transforms from a localized wake to an extended arc, which leads to a reduction in inertial drag. Consequently, the total drag force is balanced by friction-related drag, which is aligned with the direction of the cylinder's motion. The friction-related drag is in line with previous studies that focused on slowly moving cylinders. Moreover, we found that the mass flux induced by the cylinder follows a power-law relationship with the cylinder's driving speed, and this law is valid for a wide spectrum of flow regimes.

This study leverages the ATLAS3D database and observations of a low-z starburst disk galaxy (M100) to assess the impact of gas outflows on the depletion times of both the gas and the total disk during a starburst event. By combining observations of the mass and velocity of ionised and neutral gas, along with the rates of ionised absorption and ionisation in the circumgalactic medium, we estimate that ionised gas outflows increase the gas depletion time by a factor of 1.5-2. This finding highlights a previously underappreciated aspect of ATLAS3D's analysis, which had overlooked ionised and neutral gas outflows in its conclusions. Consequently, the gas and total disk depletion times of the group galaxies examined are found to be 1.6-2.5 times longer than those of the more isolated disk galaxies from the ATLAS3D survey.

Finding optimal configurations for complex systems often demands significant computational resources and time. Auto-tuning methods can speed up this process by systematically exploring various configurations to find a more efficient one. However, these methods typically rely on brute-force approaches, using linear solvers to test the impact of individual changes. In contrast, BoAnon, a novel auto-tuning tool based on constraint modeling and Boolean constraint solving, can solve the resulting models directly. By leveraging the power of modern SAT solvers, BoAnon can efficiently find a better configuration than the default, often in a matter of seconds. For instance, it can enhance the performance of existing tools, such as reducing the verification time of a protocol from multiple seconds to less than a second.

Our analysis of 2D Fourier flow coefficients in heavy-ion collisions reveals a consistent scaling behavior in the ratio of $v_n/n$ for different particles, as seen in both triangular and elliptic flow. This pattern holds for a wide range of system sizes, from oxygen to lead, and for different particle types, when normalizing within the same collisions of the same system size. This finding strongly supports hydrodynamic models that incorporate fluid dynamics driven by the initial geometry of the collisions, suggesting that $v_n/n$ may be a universal constant influenced only by the mass number of the nucleus and possibly the flow velocity.

This research addresses the challenge of quality assessment in large RDF datasets, which have been expanding rapidly over the past decade. The task of estimating the accuracy of these datasets, often referred to as computing their edit distance to a theoretical perfect version, can be computationally demanding, especially when considering all possible perfect versions of the dataset. To tackle this issue, we focus on methods that compare two instances, including the expensive exact approach and a range of heuristic methods. Our proposed solution, DistQualityAssessment, a new heuristic algorithm, lags behind the current state-of-the-heuristic techniques. However, remarkably, it rivals the accuracy of the exact approach, and in many cases, surpasses it. Moreover, DistQualityAssessment can be executed on modest hardware, making it suitable for quality assessment of moderately sized datasets.

This paper presents a novel statistical approach for modeling independent increment and markov processes. We propose using minimum density power divergence estimators as an alternative to the standard maximum likelihood estimation. These estimators provide robust parameter estimates, even in the presence of outliers or data anomalies. We show that a certain independent increment process can be used to model both independent increments and the markov property, and that its traditional maximum likelihood estimator is not consistent. To address this, we introduce an improved maximum likelihood estimate and discuss its statistical properties. Additionally, this paper investigates the weak and mean square convergence of the minimum density power divergence estimators, and an algorithm for computing it is also presented. Furthermore, this paper shows that the minimum density power divergence estimators can provide reliable parameter estimates, even in the presence of outliers, and its performance is evaluated through simulations. We also investigate the application of this estimator to real-world stock price data.
