that the level of linguistic similarity between the target and source languages
has a significant effect on the system's performance in both scenarios. As a result,
it's more beneficial to transfer knowledge from a small amount of related data in
non-target languages with high similarity, rather than from non-target languages
with less similarity.

To assess new node embedding algorithms, a reliable method is to test them on existing applications, which requires efficient evaluation of similarities between nodes and their neighbors. We created an automated framework using Python to evaluate node embeddings, featuring 18 metrics from the literature and an option for custom evaluations. To speed up the process, we developed a common suite of 50 pre-trained embeddings on 30 datasets from literature, web, and bioinformatics, which can be utilized for evaluating node embedding algorithms. The dataset includes diverse real-world nodes and features, and the project is available on GitHub.

A study of the $B^+$ decay into two $K_S K_S$ mesons is reported, based on a dataset collected at the LHC, containing 88.6 million $B^+$ mesons. This analysis allows for a detailed examination of the $B^+$ decay spectrum by splitting the dataset into three separate searches, each targeting one of the $K_S$ invariant mass distributions. A significant $S$-wave component is detected in all three searches, consistent across the entire $B^+ \to K^+ K_S K_S$ sample. The observed phase space and resonance contributions are used to study the $B$ meson polarization and confirm $CP$ symmetry. Furthermore, a direct comparison between $B^+$ and $B^-$ decels, searching for $CP$ symmetry violation. The findings are complemented by a search for $B^0$ decays into the same final state. A detailed endstation design for a low-energy magnetic spectrometer at the nTOF detector is also described, along with an outline of a research program that the upgraded detector will support. This instrument is being designed to upgrade the existing detector, taking into account the new high-intensity beam that will be available starting in 2027, to explore magnetic materials and components for future projects, including the FAsCC.

New extensions to the Standard Model, specifically one-field models with a single complex scalar field that break a global U(1) symmetry, are thoroughly examined as potential dark matter explanations. It is actually the Standard Minimal Dark Sector (SMDS) that benefits most from this analysis, where robust predictions are made for a specific primordial black hole mass range, between $10^{17}$ and $10^{20}$ grams, which could constitute all of the dark matter. These predictions are made despite uncertainties in the curvature of the potential, as long as the symmetry-breaking scale remains above a few times the Hubble scale. The smearing of the potential is found to have only a minimal impact on the predictions made, while U(1) baryogenesis is limited to very high temperature values, above $10^{10}$ GeV. The model also allows for radiative corrections to be taken into account, resulting in more than a hundred different parameter combinations to be examined. The predictions made are primarily for cases where the U(1) symmetry is not conserved, while taking dark matter to be composed solely of primordial black holes. Smaller primordial black hole mass ranges can actually contribute a small part of the total dark matter in many other different parameter configurations. A thorough graphical examination of the results made is also included.

Series elastic actuators utilize flexible sensors to measure torque at a motor, but this design introduces challenges in obtaining accurate force measurements due to nonlinearity and sensor inaccuracies, posing a significant problem for control systems in service robots. A novel algorithm has been developed to address this issue, incorporating the effects of hysteresis and sensing errors into the control loop to effectively integrate force sensing into the control process. Several existing control methods were analyzed, and it has been demonstrated that the proposed algorithm can achieve precise force tracking in tests using a single-degree-of-freedom rotational setup with a elastic sensor and motor. Compared to alternative control methods which achieved accurate position and speed tracking but resulted in inaccurate force tracking, the proposed algorithm achieved excellent force tracking performance in the experimentally evaluated system.

The interaction between expanding fluids and aggregates of particles in nature has been studied in various contexts, but peltierite provides a unique setting to observe this interaction on a micro scale. Through the expansion of lava, individual crystals in peltierite form characteristic patterns of curved boundaries and enclosed regions known as oligocrysts. To understand the formation of these features, simulations using discrete element methods were modified to account for changes in area due to the expansion of the surrounding fluid. A key factor in this study is how the competition between particles re-aggregating and the increase in distance between them influences the formation of rifts in the particle raft. The ratio of the decrease in area to the decrease in distance between particles determines the decrease in the size of the particles and affects the distance between adjacent rifts in the oligocryst. Additionally, the ratio of the decrease in area to the decrease in distance between particles can be modified by changes in the volume fraction of particles in the surrounding fluid. The relationship between the rift distances and the rate of expansion of the fluid and the particles' re-aggregation rate also plays a crucial role in forming oligocrysts with curved boundaries, which can be explained by the balance of the decrease in the particle size along the flow of the fluid.

We investigate the dynamics of multicomponent complex scalar fields on a space-time grid, where we define a set of dimensionless parameters that characterize the model. The asymptotic behavior of this system is analyzed for two scenarios: early times, where continuum theory's ultraviolet influence is minimal, and late times, where continuum theory's infrared effects dominate. Our results show a direct correlation between the lattice model's long-term behavior and the continuous theoretical flow, as evidenced by a one-to-one correspondence between the lattice and continuum theories' asymptotic states and their respective continuum theory equivalents. The system's ultimate state is determined by an initial condition and mapped to a continuum theory fixed point. We particularly highlight multiple possible end-states for systems starting in the same lattice ultraviolet fixed point. This relationship is illustrated through specific examples, including transitions between different continuum phases and the emergence of asymptotic regimes with distinct mass and interaction properties.

In this paper, a new policy optimization algorithm for stochastic environments, 
called SPGP-SARSA, is proposed, which integrates active passive positioning data 
from water robots into control theory to achieve efficient policy learning. 
A key advantage of SPGP-SARSA is its ability to accommodate real-world, 
continuous state and reward spaces, a capability lacking in many existing 
algorithm alternatives. 
To assess the performance of SPGP-SARSA, problems underwater navigations are 
formulated as stochastic navigation tasks. 
In these tasks, a water robot's objective is to reach a target location with 
accurate, passive positioning data provided by a tag. 
Our experiments demonstrate the superiority of SPGP-SARSA over prominent Alos 
and GPAlgo algorithms in these tasks.

K. S. Lashley previously demonstrated through computer simulations that the minimal comparators in sorting networks of depth 2, 3, or 4 are respectively $n \choose 2$, $n \choose 3$, and $4n-6$ for large $n$. This finding aligns with the asymptotic behavior first established by C. R. L. Hamming in 1961, who proved $n$ input sorting networks require $n \log_2 n$ comparators. However, exact values for finite sorting networks differ notably from Hamming's asymptotic values. Consequently, Las Vegas algorithms for sorting $n$ numbers, which combine the optimal comparison depth and number, will likely diverge from known values for comparison circuits. Building upon this research, this paper demonstrates that Lashley's values can be achieved through simple sorting networks, and further examines more complex comparison circuits to identify patterns.

Building upon recent developments in constructing multifluid stellar models using two distinct fluids, we demonstrate how solutions for general relativistic stellar models with multiple fluid components can be derived from solutions with a single fluid. Specifically, we focus on the conversion of one-fluid solutions to multiple-fluid solutions by examining the concepts of barotropic fluids and isentropic multicomponent models. Furthermore, we illustrate this process through a derivation of the Anisimov and Anisimov (1976) model from the Tolman (1934) II stellar solution.

In this study, we investigate the connection between bar formation in galactic disks and the characteristics of the density distribution, specifically by scaling the radius in terms of characteristic lengths, which can be derived from the vertical equilibrium and rotation curves of the density waves. To examine this connection, we used numerical simulations of self-gravitating, collisionless systems in the form of N-body particles and Gaussian functions in a disk, focusing on densities up to 10 times the maximum. The results show that bar formation is significantly influenced by the scale length of the density distribution, with the most effective bar formation occurring when the density scale length is roughly 1.5 to 2 times the scale height at the maximum density, as measured in a non-self-gravitating plane. Moreover, we observed a correlation between the efficiency of bar formation and the amount of density concentration, with more effective bar formation in more centrally concentrated systems. This study provides a framework for understanding and predicting the likelihood of bar formation in various types of galactic disks.

The formation of merger galaxies from the combining of two similar-sized galaxies is heavily influenced by magnetic fields in the interstellar and intergalactic spaces. In a series of gas-rich major mergers where the initial components had similar intensities of magnetic fields, we found that the resulting remnant's properties are instead determined primarily by its total angular momentum content, with the influence of magnetic fields found to be negligible. We found that the specific magnetic field intensity only becomes a determining factor in specific scenarios where the field intensity significantly exceeds typical values. The specific angular momentum content of these merger remnants is instead governed by the initial configuration of the magnetic fields within the intergalactic spaces, with the resulting configuration dependent on the specific morphology of the remnant. A notable outcome of this research is the potential for magnetic fields to isolate high-specific-angular-momentum gas within distinct filaments, which may subsequently influence the formation of merger rings and the overall morphology of the resulting galaxy.

This research introduces a novel 3D contrastive learning framework, referred to as 3D-CMC, for predicting the severity of wounds from their 3D point cloud data. One key challenge in this area is addressing the uneven distribution of data at different severity levels. To tackle this issue, 3D-CMC incorporates adaptive contrastive loss and sample-wise weighted cross-entropy loss. Moreover, to enhance feature diversity and improve representation, we integrate the Large-scale Pretrained Deep Network (LASA) into 3D-CMC. Our model's performance was evaluated on two distinct datasets, with notable results showing a significant improvement of 11.4% in accuracy compared to other methods on the publicly available Wound 3D dataset.

To assess whether calibrated neural network languages remain genuinely languages
despite their name, we tested a hypothesis suggesting that pre-trained models
could be efficiently fine-tuned on single-task grammar error correction.
To do this, we gathered around 10k manually created data points and employed
them to evaluate the transfer learning approach proposed, comparing it against
standard multi-task transfer learning.
The results showed our method achieved at least the same level of accuracy as
traditional multi-task transfer learning, with potential for improved performance.
We achieved this by leveraging a general-task model trained via contrastive
learning to distinguish correct and incorrect sentence pairs, while incorporating
a specific task head for fine-tuning.
Notably, using a single hundred times smaller dataset of manually created samples
of around 10k, the proposed model with gECBreeze achieved a at least the same
level of accuracy as sentence-level GEC models with 1000 times more data
manually created.
This approach yields comparable performance to large-scale fine-tuning approaches
commonly used in SOTA sentence-level GEC, while being at least a million times
more energy-efficient.
Furthermore, by building upon a general-purpose GEC foundation model, the approach
is easily extensible to multiple target languages.

A surprising finding revealed in recent research used  city-level suicide rate data in the US to test the behavioral theory of "contagion."  However, researchers had previously found conflicting evidence using state-level data.  Although it was recommended to use more granular data for this study, publicly available datasets were found to be prepackaged with rounded values to various significant figures.  To assess the impact of data collection and rounding on previous studies' results and the validity of contagion inference, we employed the US census census tract population to experimentally modify census tract-level datasets by modifying their rate values to significant figures similar to those found in publicly available datasets.  It was discovered that rounding to  one decimal place is quite common in published datasets and leads to a complete failure in replicating state-level results while producing strong evidence of contagion at the state level.  However, this finding contradicts previous studies using census data with more precise values, which showed no evidence of contagion at the state level and partly failed to reproduce it at the city level.  As a result, we conclude that the use of rounded data can lead to misleading conclusions in the analysis and that census tract-level datasets available in the US are insufficient to test the theory of contagion.

We have performed $^{155}$Gd NMR measurements on GdInO$_3$ single-crystals over a broad temperature range, which provided us with the necessary data to study the material's properties in detail. The half-quantized shift observed in the nucleus can be used to learn more about the magnetic behavior of the Gd$^{3+}$ ions, which are arranged in a cubic garnet lattice. To understand the quantity of participating Gd$^{3+}$ ions, we compared our experimental findings with theoretical calculations based on a generalized Anderson-Morels model, which yielded a result of 7.04(2), consistent with the expected value for Gd$^{3+}$ in a cubic environment. Additionally, we detected a abrupt alteration in the half-quantized shift at 20.6 K, indicating the occurrence of a magneto-elastic phase transition to a ferromagnetic state, characterized by a minute lattice distortion. To further analyze the results, we incorporated full Brillouin zone integrations into Landau-Lifshitz-Yaglom equations of motion for the 4f and 5s valence electrons. The generalised AM model's calculations for the Lande g-factor, orbital angular momentum, and magnetic ordering patterns were incorporated, which led to the observation of a coexistence of ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic states between 20.6 K and 10.4 K,

Hassidim and Knopik previously explored the round-robin protocol, a variation of the cut-and-choose algorithm employed in the self-selection process for chores. They analyzed the round-robin protocol under the assumption of $n$ players dividing $m$ items, specifically examining the relationship between the allocation produced by the round-robin protocol and that derived from the cut-and-choose algorithm, with a focus on效用比较保证. 

In our work, we expand upon their investigation by removing the restriction of duality and allowing utilities to be represent either submodular or supermodular in nature. We present an improved analysis of the round-robin protocol's performance, specifically demonstrating that for allocating $m$ items among $n$ players with supermodular utilities, the效用比较保证 can be improved to $\lceil m/n \rceil + (n-1)\lceil m/n \rceil^{-1/2}$, thereby generalizing and enhancing the findings of Hassidim and Knopik. Additionally, we prove that the $\lceil m/n \rceil + (n-1)\lceil m/n \rceil^{-1/2}$ guarantee is optimal. A similar analysis and result is also provided for the case of allocating chores with submodular utilities.

This study addresses the challenge of limited annotated data in typical semi-supervised settings by leveraging abundant unlabeled translations of a single target image. We tackle a challenging goal, given that only one view per target data point is available. Our approach to pseudo-labeling involves creating multiple versions of each difficult target data point in order to create more reliable labels. We create pseudo-labels for images that are hard to classify by translating them into multiple languages and then averaging the predictions made by each translated version. This approach has been shown to tackle a classic problem in few-shot learning by transferring knowledge from multiple views of a single target image. Our strategy has been successful in an experiment involving 100,000 images from tiny-ImageNet source classes and 6-shot test queries. We also experimented with increasing the diversity of target queries by applying random augmentation techniques, such as color jitter, which produced good results.

A comprehensive study of the UGC 8839 spiral galaxy was conducted using a combined dataset including optical and radio information, including the star formation rate, HII region population, and the distribution of these regions at various distances from the galaxy's center. In a statistically significant finding, the population of HII regions in UGC 8839 exhibits an asymmetrical pattern as it relates to the galaxy's rotational axis. This discrepancy creates a notable population difference across various galactocentric radii, particularly within the innermost 1.5 kiloparsecs, where the probability of finding an HII region is twice as high on the UGC 8839's southeast side compared to its northwest counterpart. This discovery may offer an explanation for the asymmetrical iron spins seen in type Ia supernovae within this galaxy.

The study of sub-GeV dark matter face an unique challenge, as experiments are highly sensitive to different production mechanisms which also result in different detection signatures, thereby complicating comparisons between different detectors. It is crucial to establish a consistent framework that can be applied across various paleo- and modern-detectors to make meaningful such comparisons. Paleo-detectors have a unique ability to probe extremely large dark matter target masses and tiny cross sections, offering valuable insights into the parameter space of small-scale nucleon interactions. We develop a set of cosmic dark matter flux limits using the D25D2 neo-diamond from the Namibian Neo-diamond Project and a low-background D25D2 sample, which will be utilized for analyzing a future high-durability experiment with 10 neodiamonds of 25kg each. Based on the neo-diamond data, we derive a set of sub-GeV dark matter limits and find that they are comparable to the projected sensitivity of existing and planned paleo-detectors. Looking ahead, we anticipate that neo-diamonds processed with state-of-the-art techniques could provide the most potent paleo-detector to date.

Modern databases, including social media and web search caches, are continually updated, and the update histories of these systems are often valuable and sometimes confidential. The challenge lies in reconciling the need to preserve these updates with the requirement to protect sensitive information, especially as updates can be frequent and updates from a variety of sources can be complex. To tackle this issue, we investigate the requirement to provide a public summary of the update history that does not disclose sensitive information, based on the model of differential privacy. The model of differential privacy offers a robust security guarantee, where providing a summary with differential privacy ensures that the summary will not reveal whether a specific individual included in the update history. To tackle this issue, we develop a general framework for the computation of differentially private summaries of the update histories, and we establish that the problem can be reduced to the computation of differentially private updates in a queue system. The model of the queue, however, entails infinitely many states. As a result, we propose two solutions to compute differentially private update queues, in which the first employs the Poisson arrival model, and the second does not rely on such model. In order to demonstrate the practical applicability of these reductions, we consider the computation of differentially private updates queues as an abstract machine learning problem, in which we aim to learn the parameters of the model of differential privacy updates queue that minimizes the measurement error with respect to the true, non-private metric. As a means of evaluating our approach, we employ

To understand how logical constraints within a machine learning model lead to a correct prediction, we employ minimal unsat cores in an SMT-based framework to analyze feature importance in a model, specifically for a medical image analysis model that identifies COVID-19 from CT scans.

This research addresses the challenge of automating the segmentation of surgical instruments for laparoscopic robot-assisted surgery. To address this issue, we propose a novel deep learning method, the Dual decoder attention network (DDANet). By incorporating the instrument context within the DDANet, we achieve a significant improvement in accuracy, reducing the mean intersection over union error to 0.0494 for single binary masks. The DDANet outperforms ten other pre-trained deep learning models in this task. Moreover, our instrument context encoding module can be applied to existing segmentation networks, yielding a 6.71 percentage point increase in accuracy. This research is undertaken as a benchmark for the upcoming 2020 Surgical Instrument Context Learning Challenge.

In this research, a technique is proposed, referred to as Co-Unsup, which integrates contrastive learning into unsupervised ReID studies. By pre-training a model using large-scale unsupervised data through the Co-Unsup framework, the model achieves a diverse range of reID traits. This model can then be fine-tuned with a small amount of supervised data to enhance performance. Co-Unsup is guided by the principle that the embeddings produced by a model should both capture distinction between multiple identities and diversity within each identity, respectively. To enforce diversity, a novel loss function is proposed, known as the Maximum Average Distance (MAD) loss. Furthermore, an innovative scale-map module is incorporated into the one-stage hybrid network, allowing it to generate individual instance masks and contrast them to enforce both classification and trait diversity principles. Our findings show that Co-Unsup achieves groundbreaking results, establishing new records in four benchmark tests, and significantly outperforms previous methods by a substantial margin, specifically by around 5% on the Market-1501 dataset. To support the Co-Unsup framework, a comprehensive dataset consisting of nearly 105,000 images, labeled with 114,938 segmentation masks, is also presented.

An innovative ground-testing framework is introduced to evaluate and compare
forecasting methods, specifically tailored for GARCH models in predicting value-at-risk,
and is more comprehensive than the framework proposed by Engle and Granger.
The framework's performance improvements are demonstrated through various scenarios,
utilizing a diverse range of datasets spanning multiple industries and time periods.

Using pulsar timing arrays to identify the background gravitational wave signal and its properties involves analyzing a complex parameter space. Different methods for navigating this space include Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC), Nested Sampling (NS), and a gradient-based algorithm called NPSA. To compare the performance of these methods, we simulated a non-sky-restricted pulsar timing data set with an ongoing pulsar puzzle signal and then compared their results to a maximum likelihood estimate. All methods produced comparable parameter estimates and characterised the signal effectively, with minimal differences in parametric results smaller than the uncertainties. Comparing computational efficiency, MCMC and NS exhibited similar times for a single parameter set calculation but differed significantly in total computation time due to the number of sets sampled, with NPSA outperforming the other algorithms by two to three orders of magnitude. Despite molecular dynamics implementations of MCMC providing some benefits in terms of reducing the minimum dimensionality of the puzzle, the additional increase in the number of parameter sets sampled negated this advantage, leading to no substantial improvement in total computation time for molecular dynamics MCMC in comparison to standard MCMC.

Using the LHC's opportunity to produce a rare particle and a quark simultaneously, we can create a unique research opportunity to study the color confination property of quarks. The production of this rare particle can serve as a unique signal to identify the required region of quark production. The color singlet nature of this particle ensures that its decay is directly influenced by the quark's hadronization, making it an ideal probe for this research. The main challenge to overcome for a successful experiment lies in the extremely low production rate of this rare particle. Nevertheless, the proposed research can be carried out with the current dataset from the LHC's Run 1, and it will become more feasible in the future as more data becomes available with the LHC's Run 2. The results from preliminary field tests have been consistent with the predictions made by lattice QCD, and they show a direct relationship between quark mass variations and the pion's mass changes.

Researchers studied the infrared emissions from the AcA 4380 tailings to investigate the disk around the classical T Tauri star, AcA 4380. An unusual fluctuation was detected in the star's accretion rate, varying by four orders of magnitude over nearly a year. This sudden surge in accretion resulted in a significant increase in the star's emissions across multiple wavelengths. Such variability poses a challenge to theories about disks growing or shrinking over time, as observed from distant planets, but theories about fluid dynamics and magnetic fields can account for this phenomenon. A computer simulation of the disk showed that the star's changes could be explained by fluctuations in a relatively small, unstable region, which has little effect on the overall disk structure.

The nature of luck's impact on individuals' outcomes significantly influences their reactions to the distribution system. While people generally respond positively to the ability to redistribute opportunities, they are less enthusiastic about redistributing income when luck directly determines it, due to the perceived undesirability of wasting valuable information. This effect is amplified as the variability in individuals' efforts increases. In contrast, when luck only influences opportunities, individuals value the ability to redistribute income, leading to a greater preference for such systems. These findings underscore the importance of understanding the mechanism of luck and how it affects value judgments, particularly in policy-making where such considerations have broad implications.

This study introduces a straightforward yet effective strategy to generalize stable maps from the field of complex numbers to any algebraic closure of the field with finite elements. As a consequence, significant geometric structures, such as varieties of stable maps, can be defined over fields with finite elements. By extending stable maps to algebraic settings, this research demonstrates the link between these algebraic maps' characteristic features and invariants derived from quantum K-theory through correspondences of K-theory. Furthermore, a correlation is established between invariants of stable maps over fields with finite elements and those over the field of complex numbers. Notably, this correlation yields an analytical estimation of the Euler characteristic of these algebraic maps.

Debugging data pipelines is a time-consuming and critical task in machine learning, often accounting for 50-80% of a data scientist's work. This becomes even more prevalent, representing up to 90% of the total work in data-intensive industries such as finance. Our proposed solution, DataScope, is an interactive data debugger that allows for efficient value-domain visualization and precise data value tracking to identify and diagnose data issues. Key features of DataScope include dynamic data value distribution views, interactive filtering, intuitive data tracking, and integration with popular programming languages and visualization tools. As a result, up to an 800x improvement in workflow efficiency has been observed when using DataScope in pipeline construction and data issue diagnosis tasks.

Researchers have long debated the nature of certain radio sources within the core regions of the globular cluster M15, questioning whether they are millisecond pulsars or neutron star X-ray binaries. To resolve this, we present evidence that these are actually distinct objects: a previously unidentified binary system and a highly absorbed M8204 radio source, which could be a young pulsar or a compact binary containing a millisecond pulsar. Additionally, we argue against the idea of multiple coincident millisecond pulsars in the cluster's center. These findings highlight the value of multi-wavelength analyses in understanding the properties of galaxy and cluster centers.

A major issue in analyzing network data is the reconstruction of hypergraphs from their projected views. Unfortunately, past attempts at solving this problem have either produced subpar results or proved computationally prohibitive for large-scale applications. A key obstacle in hypergraph reconstruction from its projections is a fundamental ambiguity known as the label switching problem. In this context, we introduce an innovative approach that utilizes a tailored variation of the cutting plane method to efficiently resolve this issue and achieve a highly accurate solution, even for densely connected and significantly perturbed graphs. Notably, our approach scales computationally in a way that is linear relative to the number of nodes in the graph, making it feasible for a wide range of applications.

We have developed an innovative method for calculating ultrafast laser pulses emitted in a single direction. This new approach is based on integrating short wave segments emitted at varying angles from a planar cavity. It has been confirmed through numerical experiments that we can recreate the characteristic features of directional emission by combining these segments. Furthermore, the method offers several advantages, including the ability to remove artifacts, resolution enhancement, and improved signal-to-noise ratio in simulated measurements of spectral interference patterns.

We have developed an approach to understanding how coherent light interacts with systems of atoms. Our method builds on previous work regarding the interaction of coherent light with systems of atoms that emit light. By incorporating the effects of non-classical light and non-markovian processes into our derivation of a effective description, we were able to accurately predict the scattering of probe photons in systems of atoms. Specifically, we derived the two-time second-order correlation function of the incident light, which plays a key role in understanding the scattering of coherent light and its properties. We tested our approach by examining the scattering of coherent light in systems of atoms and found that our predictions matched both numerical simulations and experimental observations, including the observation of anti-bunching in the photo-counting statistics. We also used our framework to analyze the non-markovian effects of coherent light and found the conditions under which we can accurately describe the system without incorporating the non-markovian effects.

This study focuses on offline multi-agent learning, where the goal is to find an optimal policy to maximize the total reward from available trajectory data. Offline reinforcement learning is an attractive solution, yet existing methods suffer from poor sample efficiency. To address this challenge, we introduce a new framework called SharedIndividualTrajectories (SIT). Within this framework, agents collaborate on a global memory, but maintain separate experiences. When it's time to act, they coordinate based on who's responsible for a specific state space. We developed a gradient method called SharedExperienceOptimizer (SEO) to update parameters using all available data. Our contributions include: 1) introducing the SIT framework for effective offline learning, 2) proposing the SEO method for efficient gradient updates, and 3) demonstrating through experiments on multi-agent grid worlds that SIT outperforms state-of-the-art methods by significantly speeding up convergence and achieving higher optimal returns.

This study presents a pre-trained Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) for performing rapid and accurate one-to-one (bi-univalent) image registration, utilizing label images. We propose a framework that employs two CNNs to predict forward and backward deformations between two label images, allowing for efficient inference. To ensure accuracy and prevent label overlap, we introduce an implicit energy function that guides the learning process. To validate our approach, numerical experiments are carried out on synthetic MRI brain images and real multi-modal MRI images. When applied to deforming target images with significant intensity changes and topology alterations, our proposed CNN outperforms conventional registration methods by accurately aligning images with a high degree of precision. Furthermore, to address topological defects, we introduce an innovative iterative refinement procedure that inverts the deformation on overlapping regions, thereby preventing label overlap. Numerical results indicate that this inversion strategy effectively remedies defects, thereby aligning both images. Moreover, this strategy can be easily implemented in other registration methods, providing a versatile solution to address complex topological defects.

We've discovered a link between nonlocal correlations and quantum entanglement in the realm of multispin systems. Specifically, we found that the distinction between nonlocal effects and quantum steering can be precisely entangled in certain classes of Heisenberg systems with fixed total angular momentum. Notably, we found that a difference metric between nonlocality and quantum steering is precisely entangled as it varies with the magnetic properties of the system. Additionally, this relationship can be broken, revealing a more complex correlation between nonlocality and quantum steering. This finding is significant as it reveals the interplay between nonlocal effects and entanglement in multispin systems.

The complexity and reliance on cellular and GPS devices have necessitated a higher demand for secure access, prompting the integration of Internet of Vehicles (IoVs) and IoT. IoVs, in particular, presents significant security challenges due to its vast user base and sensitive data, which could be compromised by malicious attacks. To address this issue, a novel authentication protocol has been developed, leveraging Bitcoin and IoT technologies, based on a secure wallet concept. This concept, underpinning the proposed protocol, ensures that only authorized users with secure wallets can securely perform transactions and access shared resources, providing an unalterable audit trail. A formal security analysis, utilizing the SCM model and ZMC framework, validates the protocol's robustness, while simulations and real-world implementations provide additional evidence of its effectiveness, in comparison to existing solutions, including A5, AES, and RSA, which were found to offer lower computational and communication overheads.

This study examines the pre- and post V392 Persei nova eruption using a comprehensive analysis of 18 X-ray observations, including those from the AstroSat/SDC, XMM-Newton, and XMM-Newton in 2014 and 2020. The spectral and timing spectrum analysis revealed the system's accretion state changed from an intermediate state before the eruption to a high state after. The system's high state was maintained for over five years after the eruption, with the post-eruption accretion rate at $4.6 \times 10^{-9}$ $M_{\odot} s^{-1}$ being significantly higher than the pre-eruption accretion rate of $1.4 \times 10^{-10}$ $M_{\odot} s^{-1}$. The surface brightness of the nova on the white dwarf surface was estimated to be about 100 times greater than the surrounding accretion disk. It is suggested that the nova's explosion disrupted the accretion disk and was subsequently reformed by the re-accreted material, which could have contributed to the re-accretion of the nova's ejecta and the reformation of the disk.

A technique has been developed to estimate the logical error rate of quantum circuits, building upon a new approach to assess quantum gate performance for codes related to the toric code. Logical measurements were taken for quantum circuits comprising up to 2D packed qubit layouts, and error rates were estimated by analyzing measurement data as a function of quantum gate error rates. Verification of logical protection was achieved when measuring the toric code's error rate at various levels of physical fault injection. A method using 1D measured data was also introduced to estimate the logical threshold of toric code protection. This method was used to evaluate the logical thresholds of three types of quantum gate errors, and accurate estimates were obtained for two of them.

In Massive M2M systems with limited backend support, a novel adaptive feedback encoding approach is proposed that requires minimal frontend backend interaction. Unlike traditional Lloyd algorithms that demand excessive pilot encoding and decoding between backend and frontend, this approach only necessitates minimal pilot transmission, effectively minimizing backend load. By leveraging local lattice refinement at each frontend, a refined solution is achieved without complex backend processing. Simulation results demonstrate an efficient convergence to a desired solution, solely based on minimal pilot transmission. The approach leveraged in this study can be extended to various uplink scenarios with constrained backend support.

The concept of geometric phase is being re-examined due to its significance and wide application. A comprehensive framework for calculating geometric phase is developed, showing its underlying stability across both bosonic and fermionic systems and demonstrating equivalence to previously established formulas. The newly derived expression for this approach is then applied to surface current formulas derived from the density matrix in both quantum field theories and many-body quantum mechanics, yielding a new expression for surface currents that is primarily derived from the relationship between surface currents and the geometric phase within the Schrödinger basis. Additionally, a variation of the surface current formula is obtained by considering the change in the phase of the wave function in a basis where the Hamiltonian is real and diagonal, which is then used to compute the surface current for the Tl-InAs interface and the $He_3$-$He_2$ interface.

In a precise analysis of a class of brandt-berman-bosch-van daal model within Brans-Dicke theory, we found that, generally, photons cannot reach infinite distance due to the radiation of scalar gravity, unless two specific conditions are met - either the radiation of scalar gravity is non-existent or it follows the radiation of electromagnetic radiation. We found that these conditions correspond to two of the four possible solutions the model has, and we made the remaining two solutions physically irrelevant by modifying the model's boundary conditions.

The merger rates of Population III binary black holes and neutron black hole pairs are studied using a analytical approach, considering how these pairs form in a radiation-dominated universe and considering the impact of gravitational waves on their orbits. Our model takes into account the formation of Population III stars in a uniform manner, within a range of 10 to 100 nanoseconds after the big bang, and considers the end of the radiation-dominated era. We derive the merger density rates of these binary pairs, which peak at a density of $1.6 \times 10^{-5} Gpc^{-3} yr^{-1}$ at a redshift of $z=24.5$ for black hole binaries with a mass of $49 M_{\sun}$ and an age of $\tau =12.25 Gyr$. Similarly, we find the peak merger rates of neutron-PSRs at $z=24.5$ to be $6.5 \times 10^{-5} Gpc^{-3} yr^{-1}$ for a neutron star with a mass of $25 M_{\sun}$ orbiting a $49 M_{\sun}$ black hole.

We have developed a novel device called a Gamma-Ray Burst (GRB) simulator, which is capable of accurately mimicking the unique characteristics of high-energy astrophysical bursts. This innovative simulator utilizes a rapid-switching apparatus to physically generate varying X-ray and gamma-ray energies at relatively low intensities. The device operates by mechanically modulating the gamma-ray energy input to an shielded detector from the Gamma-Ray Source (GRS), enabling precise detection of transient signals that would otherwise be ambiguous using traditional methods. The GRB simulator achieves detection times as quick as 140 $\mu$s, significantly faster than previous gamma ray burst simulation approaches. Unlike previous methods, the GRB simulator is able to mimic the variability patterns observed in high-energy bursts with high accuracy, due to its ability to directly reproduce their shape at lower intensities.

A operator T_g on the Dirichlet space is shown to be weakly compact if it is compact, but this does not hold for the Bloog space, where every compact operator is weakly compact. For 1 < p < 2, it is found that a sufficient and independent condition for T_g to be weakly compact on the Dirichlet-space D_p exists. Moreover, the strong compactness of T_g on the Bergman space A_p is proven to be equivalent to its weak compactness. We also establish that a necessary condition for the strong compactness of T_g on the Dirac-space is when T_g is compact. An example is also derived, which shows that there are functions f and g in the weighted version of the Fock space, where T_g is strongly compact while T_f is not compact. Finally, we prove that the set of functions g within a specific space, where the operator T_g is strongly compact while T_f is not compact, is not path connected.

To track the evolution of research areas within literature, a significant amount of work is required, as well as the ability to identify connected knowledge across various research fields. This can hinder the efficiency of related research. To accelerate the process and enable related scholars to assess connected knowledge within specific domains, we created a Prompting Framework that utilizes a Large Language Model, specifically GPT-3.5, to evaluate the amount of connected knowledge in literature related to a specific prompt, known as the Quantitative Index of Knowledge. This framework demonstrates the following: (1) utilizing an LSTM-based method, we achieved a quantity estimation of knowledge, resulting in improved accuracy, compared to the baseline, as validated through human annotation,; (2) utilizing the GPT-3.5's ability to process prompts, we were able to extract knowledge quantities from literature,; and and (()) most importantly, we created a user-friendly web interface that users can interact with,; (4) the framework's ability to promote efficiency, by providing the quantity estimation of knowledge, within specific research areas, as validated through user feedback,。

In this study, a two-layer, two-cell system is considered, where the first node transmits data to its corresponding receiver while being observed by the second node, in the presence of random environmental factors, and all nodes operate using superimposed amplification matrices to enhance the system's gain, and we developed mathematical formulas to measure the system's throughputs and security, and performed an in-depth analysis of power allocation strategies, showing that optimizing the system's gain requires the nodes to use equal amounts of power, and we also demonstrated the impact of power allocation on the system's throughputs and security.

A key challenge in developing secure quantum communication protocols using photon qubits is generating non-local entanglement. Here, we propose a method to create highly entangled states by combining quantum emitters with topologically-protected edge modes in a bi-directional Su-Schrieffer-Heeger lattice. Within this system, localized states at both ends become strongly interactant with the protected edge modes. By employing standard optical resonance techniques, we demonstrate that this method allows for the creation of W-states with over 60% fidelity, based on measurements of the emitted photons, according to Dirac analysis. As an extension, we illustrate that this approach can be applied to generate multi-partite entangled states, such as chain and ring states, by utilizing multiple quantum emitters and emitting photon qubits. Notably, our model does not require the complex generation of conditional entanglement through the complex interference of multiple quantum emitters, instead, it can be achieved by the standard post-selection technique.

This research focuses on how traffic lights impact the movement of automated vehicles in urban areas, especially at intersections. The study's objective is to analyze the effect of traffic signal settings, particularly yellow and red phases, on the trajectory planning of vehicles. The approach involves creating a scoring system that evaluates the impact of different signal configurations on traffic flow. Under ideal lighting conditions, the vehicle can come to a smooth stop or proceed through the intersection safely. A learning algorithm is used to optimize previous decisions, and the study's results indicate that an advanced planning method can adapt to different signal phases and find optimal trajectories.

Historically, interactive learning techniques have been hindered by the computational cost of simulating text-based virtual environments for text games, particularly when processing natural language input and output. To address this issue, we propose a highly optimized version of WorldOfZork called TextWorldExpress, which enhances processing speed by up to three orders of magnitude through a series of language-specific optimizations. Additionally, TextWorldExpress offers a general framework to accelerate simulated training for open-world learning tasks using text games and other similar domains.

Recent advancements in tensor decomposed models have opened up new possibilities for creating energy-efficient oriented hardware, specifically tailored for oriented recommendation models like FDHT. To accelerate these models, previous designs have already implemented various optimizations, such as using customized tensor kernels, reduced precision, and customized hardware. However, there is still a lack of comprehensive exploration into the topic of customized oriented hardware, such as design choices, evaluation, and comparison with traditional oriented hardware. In response, we propose a novel directed hardware architecture, FDHT-LSTM, that efficiently accelerates the FDHT- LSTM model by optimizing key design parameters, such as quantization, memory architecture, and oriented processing units. Through end-to-end evaluation, we found that our architecture outperforms existing oriented hardware designs, providing up to 3.25x more throughput, 2.25x more energy efficiency, and 2.25x smaller area, when evaluated with real-world datasets and production-like recommendations scenarios.

This study has investigated the potential of advanced data augmentation techniques, which are commonly used in computer vision, but less explored in NLP. Our research examined the use of these techniques in NLP tasks, particularly with low data quantities. Various data augmentation methods were explored, and their effects on performance with limited data were analyzed. Ultimately, our study demonstrated the promise of these techniques for NLP under low data scenarios and established a framework for evaluating the effectiveness of data augmentation techniques for training robust and generalizable models.

For theories with gravity that operate in anti-de Sitter (AdS) space, we adapt the notion of self-binding energy introduced for Minkowski space to formulate the Weak Gravity Conjecture (WGC). Our adaptation fits the framework of generalized gravity, specifically where the energy-momentum tensor follows a specific form consistent with the WGC's requirements. By examining scalar field theories in AdS, we demonstrate that the WGC in this context naturally leads to bound states at the edge of the continuous spectrum, or 'tower' as seen in Minkowski space. However, theories that adhere to the WGC in AdS would violate the WGC in Minkowski space. Furthermore, we derive the condition for the cosine of the angle between the charges of two particles that marginally satisfy the WGC in AdS based on the mass of the scalar field.

A new method for estimating multiple target states within quantum Monte Carlo simulations has been introduced. This method involves representing the target states using linear combinations of state-signature indicators, which are then optimized in an iterative process to minimize the error. Implemented via the path integral molecular dynamics approach, this method shows significant advantages over traditional techniques, such as the shift technique, in handling "fermion disasters." By representing the targets through the largest eigenvalues of the many-body Hamiltonian, the method achieves accurate results with up to 10 simultaneous targets, exhibiting better performance than shift techniques even with just 2 targets. By avoiding state orthogonalization, the method substantially reduces stochastic errors and variational biases in the projections, making it particularly effective in scenarios where the overlap between target states is high.

Let's consider a one-dimensional excellent mixed characteristic local ring, R, that is not of characteristic zero. For any integer i greater than zero, we have a specific group, $H^i_\frak p(R)$, which can be expressed as a direct sum of a reduced part and a repetitive subset. This paper defines a particular subelement within each $H^i_\frak p(R)$, denoted as $\kappa_i(\frak p)\equ e_0(H^i_\frak p(R))$. It is proven that the ring, R, is F-rational if and only if the subelement $\kappa_i(\frak p)$ is equal to $\kappa_0(\frak p)$ for all integers i greater than zero.

This paper models the relationship between participants in the electricity market and the grid operator who manages the grid, focusing on a grid operator who runs the market with an all-or-nothing order design, considering two types of supply entries. A general finding emerges, showing that a grid operator opting for an all-or-none design for the market will result in an increased amount of procurement than necessary. To illustrate the implications of this strategy, we examine two specific grid operator objectives, observing that grid reliability may suffer and that market participants may take advantage of the grid operator, in both instances.

The proof of Theorem 1 alone relies on functions of two variables, with the result of adding solutions to the equations as variables yielding Theorem 1. The paper also extends this to cases involving only one variable, with the result resembling the polynomial analogue of the Bateman-Horn conjecture, given the presence of an odd prime power n and a specific condition on a specific polynomial, given that it has no root mod p, given that it has degree d and a specific property, with a specific Galois group, with a specific odd prime power m and a specific property, with a specific Galois group, with a specific odd prime power n and a specific condition, with a specific property, with a specific Galois group, with a specific odd prime power m and a specific property, with a specific Galois group, with a specific odd prime power m and a specific property, with a specific Galois group, with a specific odd prime power m and a specific property, with a specific Galois group, with a specific odd prime power m and a specific property, with a specific Galois group, with a specific odd prime power m and a specific property, with a specific Galois group, with a specific

In the search for the Higgs boson at the Large Hadron Collider, one of the primary methods used involved a difficult-to-detect decay mode, $H\rightarrow \gamma\gamma$, and the detector in question, the ATLAS, is designed to identify this decay at an immense production rate, top quark pair annihilation, which significantly complicates the detection. The difficulty lies in distinguishing the weak force-mediated signal from the strong force-mediated process. To address this challenge, researchers are employing a technique known as jet vetoes, which filters out events containing extra quark or photon-induced particles. The difficulty here is determining whether the strategy can effectively reduce quark background without increasing false positives.

To explore new, extended scalar sectors beyond the Standard Model, we can assess the effects of additional scalar particles on the decay of the Higgs boson into two photons and the associated production process. Test cases consisting of extra scalar doublets and singlets were analyzed, and combining data from the diphoton decay and Higgsstrahlung allows for more precise constraints on the STRHCL coupling than previously thought possible. By leveraging open-space fitting techniques using combined diphoton data and a simulation of Higgsstrahlung, we demonstrate how theory uncertainties can be effectively incorporated and optimally reconciled across experiments, and we show how optimal weights for existing analyses can be determined and freely adjusted to better reflect the true correlations between results.

This research focuses on the extended North Polar Stratospheric Vortex (NPSV) that has been ongoing since 2008. We draw a comparison between this phenomenon and the polar stratospheric features seen at Saturn's South Pole during the summer of 2008. Unlike the NPSV, which is atypical for the North Pole due to ongoing planetary rotation, the polar region at Saturn is stationary during the planet's long-year-long summer. Here, we also examine the retreating North Polar season and the South Polar winter, both of which are characterized by a strong and persistent polar stratospheric and tropospherinic vortex. Observations from Hubble Space Telescope and the Cassini spacecraft are used to compare the duration of these two seasons. We find that the two seasons are similar in length, in contrast to the seasons on the Earth where the North Polar winter is longer than the summer due to an inclined orbit.

We investigate solutions to the time-dependent Schrödinger equation in a finite region of Euclidean space, focusing on a specific method to cause solutions to concentrate at a particular point and time. This method builds on the concept of potential wells, commonly used in nonlinear systems. Systems protected by symmetry often exhibit sharper convergence rates but may lack sufficient detail to describe the behavior near a symmetry-breaking collision. To address this limitation, we introduce a potential well that utilizes the full information provided by the system's associated symmetry. However, introducing this well breaks time-reversal symmetry due to the mismatch between the system's available and required components. As a result, we modify the initial conditions to maintain this imbalance, which, combined with a suitable choice of the well's strength, leads to an inevitable breakdown of the solution within a finite time.

This study introduces effective methods and tools for computing various invariants and solving specific problems in commutative algebra over fields with a character other than zero. It focuses on implementing efficient techniques for evaluating the Frob-slope field invariant, solving the Hilbert Kernel Problem in fields with a non-zero character, and calculating the Teichm\"uller series of a formal power series field extension in the context of arithmetic geometry.

A comprehensive examination of the spectral density for a strong correlation-driven insulator transition in a Hubbard model on a two-dimensional square lattice is conducted. This study utilizes the continuous-time path-integral perturbation theory to obtain the 'sum rules of spectral weight' as function of electron interaction strength. The theoretical model is applied to determine the density of states, particularly near the electron interaction strength transition point where there is a metal-insulator transition. The results obtained from perturbation theory are compared to the exact diagonalization for smaller system sizes and the density of states is also analyzed in terms of motion of an impurity to first and second order. The metal-insulator transition is shown to cause a significant disruption in the 'sum rules of spectral weight' and it is observed that higher-order perturbative contributions are necessary to restore the'sum rules of spectral weight' to their correct value.

Using one-dimensional Bose-Einstein condensates with two coupled and opposing nonlinearities, we theoretically explore the structure of quantum double dark solitons. A quantitative analysis is provided for quantum nematic states, and a new quantity is introduced to examine their density patterns. Our calculations reveal that, in this analysis, the presence of two clusters emerges in quantum double dark solitons when nonlinear interaction strength is moderate, and for higher values, it merges into a single wave packet. A numerical approach is employed to investigate the quantum double dark soliton's profile, and the results are further examined through the creation and annihilation operators, yielding supporting evidence.

This study builds on previous work concerning symplectical double vector bundles, extending it to symmetric v-fold vector bundles for any natural number v. It achieves this by first defining symplectical symmetric double vector bundles and then generalizing the framework to the v-fold case.

A recent study extends previous ideas concerning the connection between geometric and Kirillov measures, which originally applied to smooth cubic polynomial orbits within a complex simple Lie algebra $\mathfrak{sl}_2\mathbb{C}$, by exploring the connection between both types of measure in simple Lie algebras $\mathfrak{sl}_n\mathbb{C}$ for $n\geq 3$. Moreover, this research broadens an earlier result that demonstrated the statistical independence of the eigenvalues of random Hermitian matrices, specifically analyzing the geometric measure's $k$-th absolute moment for distinct values of $n$ and $k$. Notably, this investigation also establishes, for the first time, the absolute continuity of the geometric measure with respect to its coadjoint orbit's Lebesgue measure in positive-dimensional singular orbits.

We have developed an innovative algorithm capable of recovering multiple x-ray energy spectra simultaneously, even when some x-ray probes recover their targets at different energy frequencies. To achieve this, our method transforms the initial assumption of real, multi-energy x-ray spectra into an algebraic problem, which can be solved using linear and quadratic equations. By introducing constraints in the form of additional linear and quadratic equations, we modify the problem to have an optimized solution. To scale this solution to multiple x-ray probes, we use iterative least-squares methods. Our algorithm demonstrates remarkable efficiency in recovering targets with as little as a single x-ray probe, exhibiting up to an order of magnitude greater speed compared to previously established methods. Moreover, it exhibits exceptional robustness in the face of significant spectral and spatial overlapping and can accurately recover targets with distinct frequency signatures from just two x-ray probes. When dealing with targets that share similar frequency signatures, we demonstrate that adding additional measurements to our algorithm results in optimized solution accuracy.
