Determining the health status of a patient is significantly influenced by the Social Determinants of Health (SDoHa), which encompass non-medical aspects of a patient's life. While electronic health records (EHRs) provide valuable clinical and demographic data, they often fail to capture crucial SDoH information. To bridge this gap, leveraging unstructured text from notes can offer additional insights, allowing for more comprehensive SDoH data extraction and, consequently, improved patient care through targeted population health management and personalized clinical care. As a result, developing effective text mining tools with advanced machine learning models is essential for SDoH data extraction, yet these developments are hindered by the limited availability of high-quality datasets designed for this purpose. To address this challenge, our project aims to create a comprehensive dataset consisting of around 1000 notes specifically tailored for SDoH data extraction, focusing on a diverse range of topics such as housing, employment, and transportation. To ensure the extracted information's relevance and accuracy, we engaged subject matter experts including clinicians, nurses, and social workers who outlined specific extraction guidelines, annotated a random subset of our initial dataset, and offered feedback to refine the extraction guidelines, leading to the final release of the comprehensive dataset and the associated guidelines to the research community.

Often, studying time-dependent systems involves analyzing the frequency of state changes over time. When investigating rapid-switching dynamics, an underlying spatial structure can emerge, along with associated geometric features defined by the systems' rapid movement. These features can provide valuable insights into the systems' behavior during fast-switching periods. This concept is applied to analyze the efficiency of a one-dimensional swimmer, controlled by two opposing movements, and the optimal strategy to move it between two fixed positions. Our findings reveal that the control cost to relocate the swimmer between any two points is constant, leading to closed-form expressions for the cost as a function of switching speed. These expressions indicate that increased speed results in the emergence of geometric patterns, such as cusps and caustics.

The global pandemic has produced both positive and negative outcomes for urban environments. While the pandemic has caused the alteration of many urban dynamics and slowed the pace of global urbanization, it has also revealed the capacity of cities and their communities to adapt and reset. As the pandemic enters its later stages, it has become essential to assess the enduring changes in urban diversity and the shifts in urban interactions. By analyzing the long-term effects of COVID-19 on public space usage, face-to-face interactions, and the distribution of shopping patterns in a typical metropolitan area, this study has discovered both the limitations and the renewed sense of community in urban interactions. While some levels of urban diversity and face-to-face interactions have declined, it has been observed that the city's community has displayed a form of adaptability, resulting in the formation of more concentrated patterns of social connections. In order to restore and promote urban diversity, new technology can provide valuable support, such as the development of more user-friendly apps that encourage community connections, as well as more effective urban planning strategies, such as the use of decentralized ledger technology to facilitate the development of urban cryptocurrencies and facilitate more efficient resource management, as well as more robust public infrastructure, as well as more adaptable and durable public infrastructure, as well as the development of user-friendly public infrastructure, as well as the use of user-friendly public infrastructure, as well as the use of user-friendly public infrastructure, as well as the use of user-friendly public infrastructure, as well as the use of user

The Young Stellar Object V883 Orionis and its surrounding environment were observed for a year, providing a rare and detailed examination of a migrating object's impact on the inner surrounding environment of a high-mass young star. High-mass young stars typically retain a large and dynamically influential surrounding disc. Using a series of simulations, the surrounding environment near V883 Orionis was analyzed, focusing on the object's escape from the inner surrounding disc. The results show that the surrounding environment can be significantly altered by this event, providing an explanation for the observed behavior of the gaseous emission. The object's movement also influences the inner surrounding environment's structure, creating a spiral pattern that aligns with observations of the magnetic field. This study emphasizes the importance of surrounding objects in shaping the inner surrounding environment of high-mass young stars.

A scattering theory is extensively characterized through its asymptotic algebra and scattering matrix, but this approach is not universally applicable due to its reliance on a classical algebra of observables, which is not accessible in quantum field theory in position space. This issue is particularly pronounced for constructing exact scattering theories, including the Pomeranskin-Zelevinsky twist deformed $ \mathcal{N}=4 $ super Yang-Mills theory. To overcome these limitations, we establish a viable methodology for developing a precise scattering framework using correlator twist relations, extending the previously established asymptotic characterization.

The exposure people have to 5G cellular towers will differ significantly from previous generations due to 5G small cells being deployed on existing infrastructure such as commercial buildings and 5G macrocells remaining on new high gain antennas.  A model predicting human exposure from these towers has been developed, accounting for 5G cell density and attenuation within structures, a factor ignored in earlier reports.  While outdoor exposure to 5G and earlier cellular technologies is comparable, exposure within buildings will vary depending on cell density.  In areas with numerous 5G small cells, exposure inside structures may reach levels similar to older macrocell-based systems with similar average gains.  However, in areas where 5G small cells are less common, exposure within buildings could reach much higher gain levels than macrocell-based systems.  This indicates that 5G deployment's impact on exposure within structures will depend on the density of small cells, with higher exposure possible in areas with lower 5G small cell densities.

A new closure relation is introduced for shallow water waves, resulting in modifications to the commonly used shallow water approximation. These adjustments are derived from an established methodology that relates surface height to wave intensity in flat-water conditions. A specific formulation of this approach, applicable to profiles with a limited number of frequencies, is also established. A numerical implementation of this new formula is demonstrated through a square wave profile, with the implementation straightforwardly integrated into existing shallow water models. Key characteristics of the closure relation are analyzed, including its connection to alternative surface velocity formulations and prior theoretical proposals.

This article builds upon the work done in 'Surface layer theorem and Helmholtz decomposition in infinite-dimensional locally convex spaces' by J. Dolechal et al. (2020). Specifically, it enters the domain of $c_{0}(\mathbb{N})$ as a predual to $\ell_1(\mathbb{N})$ and introduces concepts related to differential forms, jet bundles, and measure projections. The main objective is to accomplish two tasks: Firstly, to define the dual space of differential forms consistent with the surface layer theorem, and secondly, to establish a measure projection theorem for differential forms. The discussion is confined to the space $c_{0}(\mathbb{N})$ for now.

A novel control system architecture for autonomous navigation has been devised for a two-dimensional environment using sound waves. The system, composed of distinct layers, includes a sound wave-based perception layer, a modeling and control layer, and a decision-making layer. The perception system collects environmental data by utilizing wave sounds, while the modeling and control system employs a reactive algorithm to process this input. The decision-making system, which includes a global path-planning component using the A* algorithm, enables the mobile platform to make informed navigation choices. Together, these layers enable precise and adaptive movement of the vehicle within a two-dimensional space using acoustic sensing and navigation techniques. Although there is currently no obstacle-avoidance function using wave sounds integrated into the system, a wave-sound-based navigation algorithm has been incorporated into the control system architecture in preparation for a future three-dimensional application.

Detecting fake news has become increasingly important due to the vast amount of information available online. To effectively detect fake news, current approaches rely on leveraging semantic and contextual information from source articles and nearby articles. Despite notable achievements by previous methods based on NLP techniques, the fake news detection task remains a challenging problem. To address this, we propose a novel approach called ContraMask, a contextual masking pre-training model that uses a pre-training task called contextual fake news detection prediction. ContraMask uses a contextual masking encoding module to handle source articles by incorporating a bio-masking encoder-decoder based on auto-encoders and a bio-masking attention-fusion network. Additionally, it considers the distribution of source sentences and their relationships with a multi-masking modeling task called sentence relationship prediction. Furthermore, ContraMask uses a multi-task learning framework to optimize both main and auxiliary tasks. Experimental results based on three large-scale datasets demonstrate the superiority of ContraMask over existing methods, confirming the value of a contextual masking pre-training model for fake news detection.

This study examines how a system's behavior is influenced by the presence of a boundary, using a model that accounts for the Bessel function. A transition to average order behavior is observed based on the rate at which the system decreases, similar to a phase change, and is defined by a critical value where the system exhibits hysteresis. This phenomenon arises from a competition between the system's internal disorder and the averaging influence of the Bessel function, resulting in an explicit Bessel hysteresis cycle. The rate at which the system decreases can be connected to the curvature of the system, and the effect of the boundary is analyzed through the change in the system's overall disorder. The rate at which the system increases is not directly experienced by the system, leading to hysteresis, and the system's behavior is analogous to that of a system in equilibrium with a heat bath. This study also demonstrates the equivalence between the system and a random walk in a potential, and the coexistence of multiple potential configurations leads to hysteresis. A critical value of the system determines the onset of hysteresis, and the system's behavior for lower values is found to be average order, and is influenced by the external system's disorder. The theoretical framework is supported by numerical calculations, and the results indicate the importance of the Bessel function in determining the system's behavior.

A promising decoding strategy for multiple access channels is decoding subspace codes, but its practical application is limited by the computational complexity of optimal methods. This research proposes a cost-effective decoding approach, outperforming existing suboptimal techniques, with an associated analysis of its performance and complexity. For finite fields, its error probability is evaluated, and the underlying decisions are modeled probabilistically to derive analytical expressions of interest. Furthermore, a simplified decision model enables the determination of the policy's associated scaling factor of computational complexity.

In this work, we address the optimization challenges of $l_1$-PCA under rotational invariance, specifically its two-block reformulation. Focusing on this problem, we develop a customized version of the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM) algorithm. Our newly proposed techniques for adapting the step size in the ADMM framework enable us to tackle larger datasets. These methods are showcased and evaluated against existing approaches in terms of their computational efficiency and performance. Additionally, we explore and demonstrate the ADMM algorithm's stability across multiple runs and its capacity for producing meaningful, interpretable results.

An underexplored direction in applying semantic labeling to any semantic task involves using paraphrase tasks to verify the consistency of annotated labels and create gold standard datasets through interactive citizen science activities. This validation approach is particularly beneficial for any semantic task that employs automatic label propagation, where the amount of required human input surges due to the necessity of verifying the correctness of each propagated annotation. In this context, we introduce a novel annotation scheme, termed consistent propagation, which incorporates the production of paraphrases as human input but enables efficient annotation propagation, resulting in a tenfold decrease in the human effort needed compared to conventional methods. This scheme is demonstrated to be effective in creating gold standard annotations for images, employing a pre-trained semantic segmentation model to illustrate its applicability.

Quantum automata recognize patterns in sequences of quantum states using quantum transducers as their model, which are extended finite-state machines, to entire sets of classical sequences, as a winning condition, and then, to determine if quantum automata can actually do so, and then, to demonstrate that certain types of winning conditions, specifically prefix-independent half-positional ones, can be reduced to.

We studied four high-variable X-ray emitters, the asynchronous polars HD 45887, HD 50208, HD 63397, and EM Persei, by obtaining new X-ray spectra from Chandra and/or XMM-Newton between October 2019 and May 2020. For all three emission lines at 6.40 keV, 6.70 keV, and above 10 keV, we found significant variability in spectra of HD 45887, HD 50208, and EM Persei. Based on the superior spectral data of standard polars, we compared the asynchronous polars' spectra and found their characteristics to be largely similar. However, the atmosphere column densities of EM Persei and HD 50208 exhibit notable variability, with EM Persei's parameters showing an especially wide range from $4.24\times10^{21}$ to $2.27\times10^{22}$ cm$^2$. In addition, we discovered a potential plasma variability above the hemispheric dividing line in EM Persei, and multiple interactions between the neutron star and the companion in EM Persei, such as a possible exosphere on the companion, a plasma confinement above the accretion column, and a possible decrease in the ionization state of the disc.

This paper outlines the setup for a complex simulation involving a fluid flow scenario, specifically solving a time-dependent Darcy flow problem, and a second problem dealing with heat distribution within a solid, time-varying domain. 

The problem is approached using a zone-based strategy, allowing the solid and fluid problems to be solved independently, with only fluid flow and heat transfer at the interface needing to be addressed jointly. 

Experimental results, solved with the FENIX software, demonstrate the performance and simplicity of this approach, allowing for a horizontal expansion of the solution domain as the simulation progresses.

To effectively manage navigation in homes and facilities with complex layouts, a comprehensive global map is typically required. However, obtaining such detailed information can be a costly process. To address this challenge, we introduce HiTMap, an innovative representation that utilizes a hierarchical approach to model both simple and highly intricate spaces. HiTMap consists of a hierarchical network of hierarchical tiles and doors, where each level network connects corresponding nodes from the parent level. Within each level network, we apply a hierarchical hidden state to model navigation at that particular granularity. By leveraging this approach, an agent can navigate between adjacent doors and switch between different level networks as needed. Trained on only a handful of trajectories, a multi-task policy based on HiTMap demonstrates remarkable efficiency, using significantly fewer computation resources than traditional global metric maps, while achieving comparable navigation performance.

Our team developed a content moderation system to identify and remove harmful content online, which leverages signals from multiple sources including text content and user reports. Our innovative text detection component and a custom feedback mechanism allowed us to efficiently categorize web content as safe or toxic. To test the system's performance on short, informal texts, we used a benchmark of Twitter messages and evaluated the results. Our basic system achieved a 0.714 F1 score on the test set. Following the deployment of the system, we observed a 0.24 probability of a user submitting a toxic report leading to the content being correctly classified as such. Although our system has been succeeded by more sophisticated text components, this research demonstrates the feasibility of a practical, multi-signaling content removal system.

Researchers achieved a remarkable sensitivity in detecting local magnetic fields, specifically a 180-attometer per second gradient, which was 9 standard deviations from the null result and four times more precise than previous best estimates. This was accomplished by combining atomic magnetometry and interferometry techniques, utilizing two ensembles of atomic rubidium separated by 12 centimeters. The experiment measured the interaction between a local magnetic field gradient and an atom's magnetic dipole moment through atomic magnetometry, and the atom's spatial distribution via atomic interferometry, all while being isolated in ultra-high vacuum and suspended by optical sheets. Although the findings are consistent with both theoretical predictions and existing evidence, they also highlight the potential for future research to explore the limits of this technique, particularly in the context of searching for varying fundamental constants.

A major challenge in creating a topological electronic heterostructure is maintaining stability against strong interactions and high conductivity simultaneously.  A novel heterostructure is proposed, consisting of a 2D contact gas of neutral spin-polarized electrons interacting with a monolayer of $CrI_3$, a magnetic van der Waals insulator.  Due to its unique properties, this structure could be controlled via an applied magnetic field, exhibiting a substantial magnetocaloric effect with the potential to display opposite responses for opposing spin states.  The heterostructure is designable to achieve equal and opposite magnetocaloric effects for spin up and down electrons, compensating the energy difference between spins and resulting in spin polarization induced by an adiabatic demagnetization process, counterbalanced only by the minimal Zeeman splitting.  This contact system is a groundbreaking concept that could pave the way for novel applications in 2D physics, requiring further research and development of fabrication techniques using molecular beam epitaxy.

An advanced statistical approach, incorporating interaction and correlation effects through a generating function, is successfully applied to modeling the complex behavior of light as it passes through randomly dispersed particles. This effective local model is capable of predicting key phenomena, including the migration of a mobility zone, the migration of an endoannulus of high intensity, the reduced backscattering, and the altered ring visibility in He-Ne laser light passing through a low-density particle suspension. By leveraging the effective gap width concept, we develop a novel local predictor of light intensity based on position and a derived electric field amplitude. This predictor accurately forecasts the mobility zone's radius and the mobility zone's on-axis intensity, which is influenced by first-order phase fluctuations. The model's predictions are corroborated by direct numerical simulations and experimental data, and it is shown that this predictor is reasonably close to non-local first-principles calculations, particularly at large transverse distances or near the sample surface.

The calculus of constructions has served as a foundational framework for a significant number of contemporary programming languages and has been a pivotal point of reference in the study of type theory since the early 1980s. This survey will delve into the history of the calculus of constructions, explore its variations and extensions, and examine the methodologies employed by Coq, the major proof assistant based on this framework.

Quantum electronics has been limited by a lack of appropriate tools to measure entanglement, as the theory of open quantum systems doesn't account for symmetry-breaking states or magnetic field effects. A new approach based on spin entanglement correlators provides a viable method for observing these phenomena in a specific class of quantum devices, including those with broken symmetries or located in environments with such conditions. This approach can also estimate the von-Neumann density-matrix entanglement, which is relevant to quantum thermodynamics, by applying it to a sample consisting of a Heisenberg chain connected to two ferromagnetic leads.

A nonparametric approach to estimating latent categorical features from observed summary statistics is developed, with a focus on exploring the impact of a Dirichlet process prior on estimating identifiable categorical weights. Through theoretical analysis and numerical simulations, we discover that using a DP prior allows for the accurate retrieval of estimable weights from the posterior mean of a mixture model, even in scenarios with high population diversity and numerous populations. This finding has the potential to refine analyses of human genetic admixture by admitting the limitations of admixture weights as a precise, objective measure.

Two-loop corrections to the Lagrangian four-point interactions are taken into account, specifically the anomalous dimensions of the three-point and four-point operators as required by quantum chromodynamics and string theory. These calculations are made for a planar limit, a key limit in which the theory can be simplified and analyzed more effectively. Furthermore, the results confirm the conjectured linear growth of the anom dimensions in the large-c limit, a limit in which the theory can be approximated more easily.

Next-Generation Silicon Optical Radar (SORar) is an advanced technique for silicon photonics that enables radio frequency (RF) signal processing. These SORar devices rely on intricate machine learning models trained through supervised methods, which in turn require efficient memory management to optimize runtime performance. Traditional GPU memory allocation methods that prioritize convenience often result in excessive memory usage. In addition, custom memory allocation strategies can be laborious to implement and may compromise safety, performance, and modularity. To address these challenges, we introduce DynaSOAr, a flexible GPU memory allocator designed to provide dynamic memory allocation while efficiently managing memory for SORar applications. By integrating with the model training and deployment process, DynaSOAr provides a comprehensive memory management framework that includes a set of application programming interfaces (APIs) for seamless memory control. To validate the effectiveness of this approach, we developed the MemeSOAr benchmark, a complex signal processing application that emulates a real SORar use case. By evaluating memory allocation strategies, our results demonstrate that DynaSOAr provides up to 2.4$\times$ improvement in memory efficiency and 1.4$\times$ improvement in performance when compared to the alternative approaches.

This study examines the generalized fractional maximal operator $\mathcal{M}_\tau$ and the fractional maximal operator with variable increments, specifically looking at how they function on generalized mixed Morrey spaces. We also investigate the $L(\vec{P})$ boundedness of these operators.

To investigate YSR states in a spin-orbit coupled system, we employed a nonequilibrium Green's function method, tailored to handle temporal asymmetry, to calculate the imaginary part of the Green's function for a ferromagnetic tunneling barrier. A Bardeen-cooper-Schrieffer model was employed, incorporating a set of YSR states resulting from a single dimer of Al and a single Al adatom placed on a superconducting Pb surface. Notably, spin-orbit coupling causes a shift in YSR peak positions, which is further modulated by the YSR state's energy and is magnified in the case of a single electron peak. Additionally, we analyzed the YSR peak splitting caused by a adatom's magnetic moment, and found that it is influenced by the magnetization and can lead to peak splitting in the presence of a single dimer.

Implicit neural style transfer has proven to be a powerful technique,
effectively avoiding the common issues associated with traditional approachest such as visual artifact problems, limited generative capabilities, and difficulties in maintaining a one-to-one mapping.
However, existing style transfer methods are generally constrained to image rendering tasks and cannot be applied to tasks like mask generation.
We introduce FourierMask, a novel implicit style transfer framework based on fourier features, that enables mask generation through a style-based method.
By leveraging a characteristic of Fourier transforms, we develop a efficient implicit formulation that leverages high-frequency style masks to introduce detailed patterns into a low-frequency target mask.
To address the challenge of enforcing a high accuracy boundary, we integrate a loss function that enforces a implicit formulation's consistency with the precise boundary of the target mask.
Through this approach, FourierMask achieves significant improvements over traditional artifact-free style transfer techniques, by enabling high-resolution mask generation via a point-cloud data structure that efficiently encodes style masks and implicitly produces dense masks.
Our method also demonstrates superior performance on complex boundary style transfer tasks, by outperforming other implicit formulations and by leveraging a loss function that enforces the consistency between the implicit formulation and the target mask's boundary.

Recent research by a collaborative team found that the complete minimal disks in 3D Euclidean space have a fully recorded collection. This finding, combined with a separate study, implies that the entire spectrum of a specific class of minimal disks in 3D Euclidean space mirrors the spectrum of parabolic cylinders in 3D. In addition, the research shows that specific frequency patterns of these disks fall within the range defined by two frequency patterns of parabolic cylinders with matching mathematical properties.

Wind turbines affect local weather patterns, which can have a significant impact 
on precipitation, particularly in areas with high cloud coverage. 
Current methods for analyzing satellite images struggle with this complexity, 
especially in remote areas. Our research addresses this challenge by introducing 
a new concept - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - a veiled core - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - a concept that encapsulates a cloud area obscured by surrounding clouds. We identify and eliminate these veiled sections by detecting and removing smaller clouds within larger ones, resulting in a refined analysis of land surface conditions. This approach allows us to accurately represent areas like the veiled core found in satellite images. By utilizing a new approach, we were able to discover and model unique features, such as a core with distinct weather patterns. This approach enables us to present a more comprehensive view of areas affected by wind turbines.

To examine the impact of a minimal low-density layer on how ions are accelerated by a negatively-chirped laser interacting with an electron target, we looked at an setup where the main laser is separated from the target by about 30$\lambda^2$ and there is a very thin ($\sim 0.05\lambda$) low-density layer right next to the target. When looking at the ion acceleration in this setup, we found that ions are given energy in a more uniform way compared to when there isn't the small low-density layer. This improvement holds whether the electron target is solid or has a certain density spread. We also looked at how increasing the size of this small low-density layer impacts the acceleration and found that the most significant gain in ion energy occurs when the radius of this small layer is about the size of the target. Additionally, this small low-density layer reduces the amount of X-rays given off by the acceleration, and it lessens the size of the density spread within the target, making it more similar to monochromatic acceleration.

A rare finding involves multiple transiting mini-Neptunes within a single star system's habitable zone, specifically within 100 solar radii. This study confirms that these planets, labeled b, c, and d, orbit a K-type star called LHS 3844, with orbital periods of 1.2 to 2.5 years. Using various methods and data sources, we determined the star's characteristics and found the planets to have small, likely rocky moons, with masses of 0.02 to 0.05 Earth masses and radii of 0.007 to 0.01 Earth radii, though further analysis with Hubble could refine these values.

We have developed a novel approach to integrate constraints into our physics-based simulations using a forward-use technique. This method leverages the inherent properties of numerical algorithms to efficiently incorporate complex constraints into simulation models. Utilizing this technique, we successfully implemented it within the framework of large-scale ab initio material simulations. This allowed us to form stable carbon-nitrogen dioxide (TiCN) by placing a carbon and a nitrogen atom adjacent to each other in the titanium dioxide material. We also found similar configurations impossible when using only a single impurity atom. We observed that the material's structural relaxation can be used to automatically identify and incorporate complex multi-body constraints. This method offers an efficient framework for integrating simple and complex constraints into simulations, which in turn can advance the study of material doping.

By combining constraints from various semi-elastic processes, we set new limits on flavor-changing neutral current (FCNC) decays of the top quark. Specifically, we impose strict upper bounds at a 95% confidence level. Where no prior limits existed, we establish new ranges for FCNC branching ratios. Notably, we limit $BR[t\to t\gamma]$ and $BR[t\to tZ]$ to very low values, as well as $BR[t\to cZ]$ and $BR[t\to cc\gamma]$ to respective ranges. These limits, derived from considering the processes $pp\to t tbar + \gamma$, $pp\to \gamma + S_0$ (where $S_0$ is a single spin-0 hadron), $pp\to Z + j$, $pp\to t\bar{t}$, and $pp\to \mu + X$ (at the LHC with an 13 TeV energy and using the ATLAS detector), reflect current limits on the FCNC couplings of the $t\bar{t}H$ and $t\bar{t}\gamma$ vertices, as well as the FCNC couplings of the $t\to ck$ and $t\to cz$ tree-level vertices, with $k$ and $z$ representing the $c$-quark and $Z$ boson respectively.

The intra-cluster medium is currently the most prominent location for the presence of heavy elements in the universe. To better understand the fundamental principles of element formation and mixing, as well as the principle of gravity as a universal regulator, researchers need to obtain a high-resolution X-ray spectral map using the X-ray Integral Field Unit (X-IFU). This study presents such an observation, which encompasses a rich cluster known as Perseus. With a comprehensive instrumental and observational approach, including deconvolution, surface modeling, forward modeling, and multi-wavelength data, we employ an exhaustive set of tools to meticulously interpret the intricate patterns of the intra-cluster medium's turbulent activity. Ultimately, these insights into the intra-cluster medium can serve as a springboard for eventual investigations into the broader principles of gravity and the operation of massive systems.

In our research, we extend previous findings by Brabek and others, as well as Zhong, to a more general context. Specifically, we establish a new lower bound constraint for an edge-coloring problem. This constraint is based on the number of edges in a graph g where the edges are colored with at least χ(f) colors more than the number of edges in a triangle. We can now confirm previous results and modify color lower bounds for various graphs, including a K4, K5, Ki,j and homeomorphic versions of these graphs.

We investigated the anisotropy in the density structure of the Central Molecular Zone (CMZ) using a novel method, analyzing the anisotropy angle derived from a elliptic model. The anisotropy angle revealed a distinct variation with scale, with the large-scale structure being elongated towards the Galactic meridian and the small-scale structure appearing more symmetric. The anisotropy angle showed a sudden shift around the 300pc scale. The findings were reinforced by analyzing the orientation of the anisotropy in the velocity field of the Local Standard of Rest. The anisotropy in the 300pc-scale structure is aligned with the Scutum-Centaurus arm, while the 30pc-scale structure is aligned with the Sagittarius spur. It is also noted that the anisotropy in the structure of the CMZ gas is consistent with the anisotropy in the velocity field.

A novel detection method for personal identification via eyewear has been proposed, which diverges from conventional techniques requiring the entire face by focusing only on the area of the eye. This new approach, named Eye-focused Detection (EFD), is designed to be a contactless solution that is user-friendly and quick to execute. The system's algorithm was refined through various experiments and can be accessed via a web interface. The source code, implemented using Python, is openly available for review on GitHub at the link: https://github.com/20280543/Eye-focused-Detection-.E.E.D.-.

This research compares the robustness of determining masses in two scenarios: for a single qubit and a single qutbit affected by either amplitude damping or phase-diffusion-type decoherence. Initially, we establish general formulas for the time required to achieve a specific tolerance level of ambiguity in mass determination for both systems. Subsequently, we perform a detailed analysis of the time needed to reach an arbitrarily small tolerance level of ambiguity for each scenario under the given type of decoherence. The results indicate that, in the case of amplitude and phase-diffusion-type decoherence, qutrits have an advantage over qubits by determining masses with a shorter time frame. Notably, under the amplitude-decoherence channel, our theorems show a distinct disparity in this advantage, as the time needed to achieve an arbitrarily small ambiguity tolerance is finite for amplitude-decoherence but infinite for phase-decoherence for both systems.

Our recent discoveries indicate that the positrons produced by a Bernese metal vapor (BMV) type-II target have a total energy distribution of approximately 3.5 keV and a minimum threshold of around 1.5 keV. Additionally, our findings reveal a threshold at approximately 15 keV for the positron energy. By adjusting the magnetic field in front of the BMV device, we observed a shift in the low-energy positron threshold, which also changed from highly polarized to less polarized. Specifically, we found that the positrons with a total energy of approximately 3.5 keV can be controlled and directed, with a degree of polarization exceeding 30%. Achieving a higher degree of polarization in a large number of high-energy positrons would be a significant breakthrough, potentially enabling several beneficial applications. Furthermore, the BMV device offers a cost-effective and relatively simple solution for generating a positron beam, with the potential to be scaled down for research and medical applications.

We have developed a novel approach to modify the Grigorchuk group G, resulting in an infinite sequence of distinct polynomial diameter groups D_i, denoted D_i, derived from the same base G. Specifically, each group D_i exhibits shared characteristics with G, such as having countably many nilpotent subgroups, a countable number of conjugacy classes, and a countable number of finite quotients. Nevertheless, D_i can be obtained from G by altering a single relation in its presentation. Moreover, there exists a countable number of other groups G_j that can be derived from G by changing just one relation and exhibit exponential diameter. As a result, in the topological landscape of the orbit space of 4-generated 2-relational presentations, groups with polynomial and exponential diameter are situated in adjacent locations.

This research focuses on designing a precise temperature measurement system based on the frequency-dependent base period of a relaxation oscillator. The circuit operates without the need for high-voltage sources, consuming less than 100 microamperes. The prototype was built using 55-nanometer complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor (CMOS) technology, and the resulting frequency output shows a 200-microhertz / degree Celsius sensitivity and exhibits minimal nonlinearity, with deviations under 0.5 degrees Celsius across the -20 to +50 degrees Celsius temperature range.

A one-fluid model is utilized to examine the stability of a non-axisymmetric equilibrium in a star, where the fluid is contained by a magnetic field shaped like a torus. This equilibrium is achieved through the mutual support of current components: one running along a toroidal direction, and another running along a poloidal direction, with the latter being maintained by the pressure of the star and the effects of magnetic tension. When analyzing non-axisymmetric disturbances, it's found that the star's surface and a critical value of the toroidal current component play a pivotal role in determining stability. In cases where the toroidal current is below this critical value, the equilibrium reverts to its poloidal state; however, when the current exceeds this critical value, the stability is maintained as a toroidal configuration, showcasing the ability of these opposing modes to switch between states, potentially serving a similar function to a positive feedback mechanism in a magnetic dynamo.

When exact RG flow equations are available, they can be transformed into a set of PDEs resembling the fluid dynamics equations, and this connection might provide fresh perspectives on RG flows' inherent irreversibility. By linking the gradient of the RG beta function to the energy dissipation in a fluid, we can use the analogy between the two systems to formulate conjectures about the relationship between the information lost in the RG flow and the amount of energy dissipated by the corresponding fluid. A key aspect of this connection is that both the information loss in the RG flow and the energy dissipation in the fluid are determined by the same irrelevance scales, or 'cut-off', reinforcing the idea that a field theory can be viewed as the historical record of a fluid's evolution. This connection has been explored in detail for the k-step generalizations of the Wilsonian RG, which are themselves interconnected through 'sonic horizons' that connect the Wilsonian flow to the conformal point. For a specific choice of fluid speed, these 'sonic horizons' are located at the k-step generalizations of the Wilsonian flow's irrelevance scales, and the location of the 'sonic horizon' is linked to the entanglement entropy of a region in space whose size is comparable to the 'irrelevant operator's' scaling dimension.

When searching for music lyrics or audio, a search engine can significantly expedite the process compared to standard web searches by presenting relevant results more efficiently. To fulfill this requirement, the task at hand is to retrieve music tracks from several databases based on partially provided lyrics. To tackle this challenge, the solution proposed involves initially identifying relevant songs from a limited set of several hundred candidates using Chroma, a music-embeddings technique, and then performing a detailed content comparison for each song's lyrics. This approach has shown remarkable accuracy, achieving near 100% correctness in full-scale tests with a provided dataset. Moreover, the proposed method outperforms common alternatives, such as text-based searches like ABIS or RISE, by more than 2% in precise matches.

We demonstrate that certain short exact sequences associated with topological groupoids, which represent gerbes over topological stacks, correspond to specific cohomology classes defined over those stacks.

To build a significant number of massive stars, molecular cores must remain and continue to grow over time. In order to understand this requirement, we analyzed the growth and structure of dark regions in a well-documented, actively forming cloud, compared with each other and with corresponding molecular cores. We discovered that the dark regions generally exhibit a short lifespan, as well as a low and varying mass growth rate, indicating a struggle to create several generations of massive stars within the Taurus cloud. Utilizing a well-established relationship between mass and radius in an expanding bubble model, we found a generally constant radius growth rate, as well as a larger size variance, in dark regions when there was evidence of multiple core generations coexisting. This indicates that modifying the model to account for the influence of radiation from massive stars on the surrounding medium, along with adopting a power law distribution of bubble sizes, may help address the issue of core longevity and mass growth necessary for the formation of multiple massive stars.

The duality between G"odel algebras and certain distributive lattices has been utilized to represent finitely generated G"odel algebras. Through Chon"i's/duality theory, we establish a correspondence between four-square lattices within the duality of finite G"odel algebras and finite forests. This relationship allows for a transformation from finite forests to G"odel algebras and conversely, from G"odel algebras to forests. Notably, certain properties such as the commutativity of operations in finite forests and the common leftmost element in three consecutive operations in G"odel algebras are preserved under these transformations.

A 3D point cloud LiDAR classification task is typically assigned a single class label to each associated feature point, but this task can be made more complex by assigning a different class label to each point. Research has shown that point cloud classification accuracy significantly improves when neighboring points are taken into account, yet existing methods are hindered by the sparsity of label annotations. To tackle this issue, a novel approach is proposed that leverages a graph convolution network to incorporate local contextual information, despite the limited availability of labels. This is achieved by utilizing a position-based feature to represent each point and its neighboring connections, and by training a dense decoder to regenerate the missing labels. To efficiently train this approach, a small dataset is collected to create a teacher model, which provides weak supervision through the comparison of predicted and actual teacher labels. The results indicate that the proposed method outperforms existing solutions in several benchmark datasets, demonstrating the effectiveness of using contextual information for accurate classification, despite the limited availability of labels.

This study focuses on the preservation of posdefinity in zonal functions through differentiation and integration, and provides an explicit definition of fractional-order zonal function differentiation and integration. A key consequence of defining fractional-order zonal function differentiation and integration is that it can effectively remove the posdefinity of a zonal function.

We have developed a quantitative assessment method for the wall roughness in finite-sized foams in motion, which is defined as the ratio between the microscopic length scale, representing the average radius of plate bubbles, to the macroscopic length scale. Using a quantitative analysis technique, we verify the $1/7$ power law within the microscopic scale and investigate the impact of wall roughness on the flow within a foam.

Deep learning techniques using convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have surpassed traditional methods in image recognition, but the high computational costs and memory requirements of CNNs make them impractical for many devices. One effective solution is using ensemble classifiers with smaller, more efficient lightweight neural networks, which offer improved accuracy and lower processing costs. However, designing and training these ensemble classifiers manually is a time-consuming and labor-intensive process. Our proposed solution is an automated algorithm that uses genetic algorithms to create high-performance ensemble classifiers with minimal human input, demonstrating superior results to existing methods.

In a rotating Hele-Shaw cell filled with a liquid, the boundary between two non-mixing liquids can exhibit different behaviors depending on tension. By analyzing the system, we found that low membrane tension leads to a non-equilibrium, tree-like structure, while high tension results in a smooth circle. A moderate Membrane tension results in a radiately symmetric instability that can either remain stable or evolve into a higher number of peaks of instability. This research relies on a robust set of experiments, verified through imaging, fluid dynamics simulations, and theoretical analysis. We define a new parameter, $\tau$, representing membrane tension in relation to inertial forces at a given angular velocity, and observe that tension determines the stability of different states in the rotating Hele-Shaw cell. At low $\tau$, a tree-like structure is prevalent, while at high $\tau$, a smooth circle is prevalent. A radiately symmetric instability emerges at moderate $\tau$, and increasing $\tau$ within this range causes the formation of peaks of instability that can either remain stable or become unstable and lead to a transition to a smooth circle. This research reveals the influence of membrane tension on the behavior of the liquid's boundary in the rotating Hele-Shaw cell.

A new understanding of work in statistical thermodynamics is proposed, which aligns with the Jarzynski equality and remains consistent with traditional definitions. According to this view, work done on a system during an isolated evolution can be seen as a sum of macroscopic work and a secondary, internal component affecting a system's microstate. The new framework enables a quantitative analysis of work's stochastic nature and its impact on a system's equilibrium distribution following a sudden change. The framework also paves the way for studying how non-equilibrium effects influence physical properties like diffusion due to toggled interactions.

We utilized the Submillimeter Array and Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array to observe a set of complex hydrocarbon molecules within the TMC-1 interstellar cloud. Specifically, we measured the absolute abundance ratios of two molecules, cycopentadiene and benzene, by comparing isotopologues within each species. In spectral observations, we found the absorption feature of a cycopentadiene species, ethynyl-cyclopentadiene (CCH), and found its abundance in relation to a cyanogen derivative, specifically 1.5 to 2 times higher than its benzene counterpart C3H/C2H ratio. To the best of our knowledge, this is the initial instance where the comparative CCH to CN abundance has been determined for both cycopentadiene and benzene, or where cycopentadiene species have been detected in the TMC-1 interstellar cloud.

This paper presents a novel look-ahead attention machine translation model that allows the encoder to translate tokens to be attended to by the decoder in the current time step in advance, resulting in improved attention patterns and better translation results. To build upon this, we also introduce a multi-step look-ahead attention model that enables the decoder to attend to a larger look-ahead range in each time step. Our findings show that even a small look-ahead range leads to significant increases in BLEU scores, a look-ahead attention model outperforms the traditional attention model, and the ability to look ahead R tokens results in better attention patterns and higher BLEU scores, with R being any value from 1 to the entire target sentence length.

The European grid project's completion in 2008 marks the beginning of a new phase in its history. This paper explores how a global approach can facilitate planning and progress in grid computing. It details the development of a policy for the progress of the grid computer in Europe, showcasing the creation and implementation of a progress plan through a collaborative approach involving multiple stakeholders. This approach showcases the benefits of a collaborative approach in developing a policy that can be applied to other projects and initiatives.

A new class of anisotropic cosmological models based on Kosul connection with non-metric compatibility has been introduced to address the limitations of the 1960s anisotropic model. This modification allows for a more accurate representation of the universe's evolution by incorporating a variety of anisotropic models. Using a state equation for a perfect fluid, we solve the corresponding gravitational equations and provide a general expression for the model's geometric properties. Statistical analysis of radio galaxy distribution data leads to estimates for the model's viscosity coefficient, which is found to be finite and in compliance with theoretical limits. Anisotropy in this model is directly related to the presence of shear, and a comparison with observational data supports the validity of these predictions. Finally, the model's behavior is examined through time-based graphical representations.

Peers have a significant impact on shaping an individual's inquisitiveness, and this influence is reflected in how curiosity spreads within communities. However, current methods for predicting curiosity rely solely on historical data, ignoring the role of peer interaction. To bridge this gap, we propose a new model called Curiosity Prediction via Peer Influence (CP^2), which incorporates peer influence into curiosity prediction. At the core of our model lies a curiosity evaluation module, complemented by peer influence components that model both macro and micro levels of influence. We test our model using two datasets and demonstrate its accuracy in capturing peer impact and predicting curiosity, showing substantial improvements over existing baselines.

We have developed a mini-batch and non-conjugate learning-capable version of graph Matérn Gaussian processes. By approximating its complex fractional Laplacian operator with graph Laplacian, we have achieved a significant reduction in computational complexity to O(n log n). This enables us to utilize efficient methods such as the conjugate gradient method with limited iterations for solving linear systems during optimization. Our approximation preserves the smoothness characteristics of the original Matérn family, offering a level of differentiability that exceeds that of the Whittle-Marron approximation. We have validated our approach on various functions within the Matérn family and demonstrated notable performance, particularly for functions requiring high differentiability. Furthermore, we have explored an innovation where multiple discrete original Matérn family functions can be modeled using a single Gaussian process, facilitating efficient learning even with a singular precision parameter set.

Urban sensor deployment for effective traffic management is crucial, particularly with the increasing popularity of ridesourcing vehicles. This study utilizes these vehicles to cover roads and collect data, particularly in an urban setting. A sensing coverage problem was defined to determine the most comprehensive data collection possible with ridesourcing vehicles subject to certain constraints. Various coverage metrics were introduced to evaluate the effectiveness of the coverage problem, and it turned out that the reliability of data collection with ridesourcing vehicles depends on multiple factors, including the number of vehicles used and their individual coverage probabilities. A mathematical model was developed to maximize the comprehensive data collection subject to certain constraints, including the number of times each sensor was covered and the available vehicles. This model was broken down into two simpler models to efficiently find the best solution. Furthermore, a new algorithm was devised called VHG and used in practical scenarios to demonstrate the accuracy of the coverage metrics and the performance of VHG. The results showed that VHG performs well even with a limited number of vehicles, particularly along major roadways.

Our study explores the implications of limits set by $J/\psi \to \text{invisible}$ decays on dark matter-nucleon scattering cross sections, specifically considering final states consisting of neutrinos or stable invisible particles, potentially including galactic axions, in addition to any new light vectors or scalars that could lead to J/psi decays into invisible states. We establish novel constraints from $J/\psi$ data, obtaining limits as tight as $1.4 \times 10^{-20}\,\text{fm}^2\,\text{fm}^2\,\text{GeV}^{-2}$ for a scalar mediated by an $\eta$-mixing and $5.6 \times 10^{-22}\,\text{fm}^2\,\\text{GeV}^{-2}$ for a new vector in the absence of $\eta$-mixing, narrowing the limits to $1.4 \times 10^{-21}\,\text{fm}^2\,\text{fm}^2\,\text{GeV}^2$ and $5.6 \times 10^{-21}\,\text{fm}^2\,\text{fm}^2\,\text{GeV}^{-2}$ respectively, when taking into account the possibility of dark matter composed of a mixture of the axion and the new gauge boson. We also consider the production of dark matter

Recent research has shown that self-adjoint variable stepsize splitting methods, or SGLMs, have excellent second-order accuracy and good stability, especially for solving systems of differential equations with negative real parts. Although SGLMs have been successfully implemented using uniform time steps, their application with non-uniform time steps, especially in solving systems on non-uniform spatial grids, results in a complex, time-coupled difference equation. This equation is not just an algebraic expression, but a pentadiagonal matrix that changes with each time step. Despite various reduction techniques, existing methods fail to maintain the SGLM's second-order accuracy, usually dropping to first-order accuracy. This research presents a new approach that achieves the desired second-order accuracy accuracy by splitting the matrix into two parts and using the Thomas algorithm to solve the resulting equations, all while staying within the realm of SGLM's characteristics. This approach is demonstrated through a convection-diffusion problem using the Lax-Wendroff scheme for spatial discretization, showing a significant decrease in the error to approximately 10^-5 compared to 10^-3 with a previously used method.

The Minimum MFSSA minimum MFSSA algorithm is now available for implementation on the internet through a new web interface, specifically the minimum minimum MFSSA web algorithm, which was created using the StackAdapt library and can be accessed at http://stackadapt.com/minmfssa/. This user-friendly tool allows users to input data directly into their web browsers and obtain the minimum minimum MFSSA results, which can be copy-pasted or downloaded in the form of a CSV file. To make the best use of this tool, it is recommended to access it from a computer with a modern web browser, such as Chrome, Firefox, Safari, or Edge. The source for this tool is located in the StackAdapt repository, and it is licensed under the terms of the GNU General Public License version 3, which allows for free use, modification, and distribution, subject to the attribution requirements specified in the license. The minimum minimum MFSSA web algorithm tool is now available for download at the following URL, http://stackadapt.github.io/minMFSSAWeb/,.

The task of essay scoring for items such as college board exams involves assessing a vast number of items daily, making it crucial for scoring systems to be both efficient and reliable. However, the black-box nature of deep learning-based autscoring models poses a challenge, as it becomes difficult to understand the rationale behind their predictions. This study leverages interpretable machine learning techniques to analyze these models and the data they work with, resulting in the discovery of two key issues: the algorithms exhibit excessive sensitivity to minor input changes, and they display overstable patterns where they rely too heavily on specific word associations. These findings suggest the algorithm's scoring method diverges from human raters and call for score discrepancies to be accounted for, as well as the development of more transparent and reliable autscoring models.

This study examines the long-term behavior of the random walk denoted as S_n with independent, identically distributed increments having a mean of zero and a standard deviation of one. The behavior of the random walk, in question, falls under the category of heavy-tailed distributions, specifically with a tail index of one, and is influenced by the probability density function of the positive tail, denoted as F̄_+. A nuanced analysis is undertaken to explore the effects of additional parameters (denoted as 'b' and '\gamma') on the asymptotic behavior, and three distinct regimes are defined based on these parameters. The nomenclature of these regimes is inspired by Donsker's and Yor's exceptional processes, and for each regime, the paper derives specific asymptotic formulas for the joint distribution of the absolute value of the random walk and its sign at time t. Notably, the formula for the distribution becomes more intricate in some cases, and includes an exponential factor in a particular regime. To validate the robustness of these findings, numerical simulations are incorporated into the analysis.

The success of biological control relies on maintaining a high level of entomopathogenic nematodes relative to the birth rate of the target insect. This relationship between nematodes and insects has traditionally been studied through laboratory experiments using controlled populations. However, the behavior of these organisms changes when they are released into the environment. A general mathematical model has been developed to address this issue by incorporating spatial and temporal dynamics, as well as the movement patterns of both nematodes and insects. A detailed analysis of the model reveals critical thresholds that determine the outcomes. These thresholds include conditions for the existence of steady states and the stability of disease-free and infected cycles, as well as the potential for sustained oscillations in the population dynamics. A corresponding strategy has been developed to identify the factors influencing these cycles and their stability, along with an empirical approach to estimate these factors through laboratory data. Numerical simulations have been used to validate these predictions.

A widely adopted method for training deep learning networks, known as knowledge distillation, involves a small, high-performance network learning from a larger network. While generally effective, our research into automatic nucleus detection using deep learning revealed that the typical teacher-student configuration has limitations. We observed that each connected component of a nucleus is individually segmented by the standard approach, rather than each distinct part being correctly identified as separate from one another. To address this issue, we developed a novel 'W-shaped' network, where an additional teacher and student network are added, creating three additional valleys in the combined output. The results indicate that this innovative design achieves superior performance, matching the accuracy of the current state-of-the-art while reducing the required computational power by 40% in terms of parameters.

This study examines the rank twists of local factors in the context of representations associated with odd special orthogonal or symplectic groups. We demonstrate that the combined rank of these twist factors reflects the isomorphism between the underlying representations, a conclusion that aligns with the Langlands conjecture.

A collection of partially observed Hamiltonian paths within a graph G, whose vertices are a subset of G's vertices, can efficiently locate any vertex in G by forming an identifying code if and only if the graph does not have a symmetric structure that would confuse the location of a specific vertex. We propose a new metric, the Hamiltonian path index, based on the minimum number of partial observations needed to achieve this location, and this index is is invariant for graphs that have a certain symmetric structure. This new index is related to the traditional concept of identifying codes and has a mathematical formula that can be calculated from the existing part paths.

It is becoming more clear that a significant number of patients with COVID-19 die due to a shift from an inflammatory cell death, characterized by a shift to necrotic or necroapoptotic cell death and a collapse of the immune system. Based on this finding, it suggests that anti-inflammatory medications might have the unintended consequence of prolonging the life of infected cells and promoting a more beneficial form of apoptotic cell death. It is crucial to consider that certain classes of anti-inflammatory medications have been shown to interfere with both inflammatory and non-inflammatory cell death pathways. As such, it is necessary to reassess the use of such medications, as some may have a restricted effect on non-inflammatory cell death. Given the lack of such specificity exhibited by widely used anti-inflammatory medications like hydroxychloroquine, it seems that such drugs should be avoided. In contrast, dapsone, another medication within the same class, displays a more limited effect on non-inflammatory cell death pathways. As such, it might be a more effective treatment option. Moreover, COVID-19 has been shown to induce a significant number of tumors due to a shift to necrotic and necroapoptotic cell death. This paper outlines a methodical approach to identifying exogenous variables through causal instrumentinequalities, which can be applied within the framework of partial observability and reinforcement learning.

By incorporating the concept of latent states and treating them as variables influenced only from outside, this method enables simpler observations while maintaining the original complexity of the underlying system.

It is within this new understanding that the algorithmic process of finding the smallest set of influencing factors - or the optimal causal instrument inequalities - is made possible.

It is shown that doing so results in an policy that is as effective as the one derived from the original complex model.

Furthermore, this paper presents the cognitive - or Causal Instrumentinequality Partial observability Markov Decision process - a mathematical representation of the situation being described.

It is with this new mathematical framework that the algorithmic process of finding the smallest set of influencing factors is made possible.

It is proposed that this approach can be seen as a form of data-driven theory formation, which allows the agent to develop an intuitive grasp of the underlying system by recognizing patterns in the data.

It is beneficial for partial observability Markov decision processes, which are a type of mathematical representation used to model complex systems.

It is through this approach that the agent is able to recognize patterns in the data and develop an understanding of the underlying system.
